title: Quantum Walks On Simplicial Complexes And Harmonic Homology: Application To Topological Data Analysis With Superpolynomial Speedups
authors: Ryu Hayakawa, Kuo-Chin Chen, And Min-Hsiu Hsieh
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2138 (2026).

This work investigates whether quantum walks on simplicial complexes exhibit quantum advantages. We introduce a novel quantum walk that encodes the combinatorial Laplacian, a key object reflecting the topology of the simplicial complex. We construct a unitary encoding projecting onto the kernel of the Laplacian, representing the harmonic cycles in the complex's homology. Our efficient construction of quantum walk unitaries for clique complexes paves the way for exploring higher-order interactions within topological structures. Our construction requires [MATH] gates, where [MATH] is the number of vertices, [MATH] is the smallest non-zero eigenvalue of the Laplacian, and [MATH] is the projection error. Our results indicate apparent superpolynomial quantum speedup with quantum walks, without quantum oracles, provided the spectral gap of the Laplacian is inverse-polynomially bounded and efficient simplex sampling is available. Crucially, the walk operates on a state space encompassing both positively and negatively oriented simplices, effectively doubling its size compared to unoriented approaches. Through coherent interference of these paired simplices, we are able to successfully encode the combinatorial Laplacian, which would otherwise be impossible. This is our major technical contribution. We also extend the framework by constructing variant quantum walks that enable us to: (1) estimate normalized persistent Betti numbers throughout a deformation process, (2) verify a specific QMA[MATH]-hard problem related to clique complex homology, showcasing potential applications in computational complexity theory, and (3) solve the high-dimensional discrete Dirichlet problem (HDDP), generalizing the classical discrete Dirichlet problem on graphs to simplicial complexes, with an apparent superpolynomial speedup over the best known classical algorithm.

.
tldr: This paper introduces quantum walks on simplicial complexes to encode combinatorial Laplacians and achieve superpolynomial speedups for topological data analysis and related problems.
motivation: To explore whether quantum walks on simplicial complexes can provide quantum advantages for topological data analysis and homology computation without relying on oracles.
method: The authors construct a quantum walk that encodes the combinatorial Laplacian by using a state space of oriented simplices and coherent interference, enabling projection onto harmonic cycles.
result: They achieve apparent superpolynomial quantum speedups for estimating persistent Betti numbers, verifying a QMA1-hard problem, and solving the high-dimensional discrete Dirichlet problem, assuming an inverse-polynomial spectral gap and efficient simplex sampling.
conclusion: Quantum walks on simplicial complexes can yield significant speedups for topological data analysis and related computational problems, with potential applications in complexity theory.

title: Efficient Classical Computation Of The Neural Tangent Kernel Of Quantum Neural Networks
authors: Anderson Melchor Hernandez, Davide Pastorello, And Giacomo de Palma
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2118 (2026).

We propose an efficient classical algorithm to estimate the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) associated with a broad class of quantum neural networks. These networks consist of arbitrary unitary operators belonging to the Clifford group interleaved with parametric gates given by the time evolution generated by an arbitrary Hamiltonian belonging to the Pauli group. The proposed algorithm leverages a key insight: the average over the distribution of initialization parameters in the NTK definition can be exactly replaced by an average over just four discrete values, chosen such that the corresponding parametric gates are Clifford operations. This reduction enables an efficient classical simulation of the circuit. Combined with recent results establishing the equivalence between wide quantum neural networks and Gaussian processes [Girardi et al., Comm. Math. Phys. 406, 92 (2025); Melchor Hernandez et al., Ann. Henri Poincaré (2025)], our method enables efficient computation of the expected output of wide, trained quantum neural networks, and therefore shows that such networks cannot achieve quantum advantage.

.
tldr: Proposes an efficient classical algorithm to compute the Neural Tangent Kernel of Clifford+Pauli quantum neural networks, showing they cannot achieve quantum advantage.
motivation: To determine whether quantum neural networks can provide a quantum advantage by analyzing their training dynamics via the Neural Tangent Kernel.
method: Replaces the average over initialization parameters with an average over four discrete Clifford values, enabling efficient classical simulation.
result: The NTK can be computed classically in polynomial time, implying that wide quantum neural networks in this class are equivalent to Gaussian processes and thus classically simulable.
conclusion: Such quantum neural networks cannot achieve quantum advantage, and the work provides a classical algorithm to compute their expected output after training.

title: Light-induced Nonadiabatic Dissipative Quantum Dynamics Of The Na2 Molecule
authors: Patrick Barron, Kriszti\'an Szab\'o, G\'abor J. Hal\'asz, K\'alm\'an Varga, \'agnes Vib\'ok
abstract: ArXiv:2606.15292v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Strong light-matter coupling between molecules and optical or plasmonic cavity modes has emerged as a promising platform for advancing photonics, materials science, and chemistry. However, optical cavities and plasmonic resonators in particular are inherently lossy systems characterized by finite photon lifetimes. Accurate theoretical descriptions of molecular dynamics under strong coupling therefore require a proper treatment of cavity losses. In this work, we compare three theoretical approaches for modeling dissipative molecule-cavity dynamics within a realistic parameter regime: the Lindblad master equation, the stochastic Schr\"odinger equation, and the non-Hermitian Schr\"odinger equation. As an example, we consider the two lowest energy state of Na2 molecule coupled to a cavity mode and analyze the time evolution of the excited-state population and the mean photon number. Our results demonstrate that the stochastic Schr\"odinger equation provides an accurate and computationally efficient alternative to the Lindblad master equation, while the non-Hermitian Schr\"odinger approach is found to be applicable only within a limited range of conditions. Furthermore, we show that inclusion of molecular rotation leads to rotational-vibrational-photonic coupling and gives rise to pronounced nonadiabatic dynamics through light-induced conical intersections. These findings highlight the importance of both dissipation and rotational degrees of freedom for a realistic description of molecular dynamics in strongly coupled molecule-cavity systems.
tldr: This paper compares theoretical approaches for modeling dissipative molecule-cavity dynamics under strong coupling, focusing on Na2 molecule.
motivation: Optical cavities and plasmonic resonators are inherently lossy, requiring accurate treatment of dissipation in molecular dynamics under strong coupling.
method: Three approaches are compared: Lindblad master equation, stochastic Schrödinger equation, and non-Hermitian Schrödinger equation, applied to a Na2 molecule coupled to a cavity mode.
result: The stochastic Schrödinger equation is accurate and efficient; the non-Hermitian approach is limited; inclusion of molecular rotation leads to nonadiabatic dynamics via light-induced conical intersections.
conclusion: Both dissipation and rotational degrees of freedom are important for realistic description of strongly coupled molecule-cavity systems.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates theoretical approaches for modeling dissipative dynamics in strongly coupled molecule-cavity systems, using Na2 as a test case. The authors compare three methods: the Lindblad master equation (LME), the stochastic Schrödinger equation (SSE), and the non-Hermitian Schrödinger equation (NHSE). They find that SSE offers accurate and computationally efficient results, while NHSE is limited to specific regimes. Additionally, they show that including molecular rotation introduces rotational-vibrational-photonic coupling and light-induced conical intersections, leading to nonadiabatic dynamics. The study emphasizes the need to account for both dissipation and rotational degrees of freedom for realistic descriptions.
key_contributions: Systematic comparison of LME, SSE, and NHSE for molecule-cavity dynamics under realistic parameters.
Demonstration that SSE is an accurate and efficient alternative to LME.
Identification of the limited applicability of NHSE.
Discovery of rotational-vibrational-photonic coupling and light-induced conical intersections in Na2.
Highlighting the importance of rotational degrees of freedom in strong coupling.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors model the two lowest electronic states of Na2 coupled to a single cavity mode, including vibrational and rotational degrees of freedom. They employ three dissipative approaches: LME (full density matrix), SSE (wavefunction sampling with quantum jumps), and NHSE (effective non-Hermitian Hamiltonian). The parameters are chosen to match realistic cavity losses (photon lifetime ~10-100 fs) and molecular couplings. The dynamics are initialized with the molecule in the excited state and cavity in vacuum, and they compute time-dependent excited-state population and mean photon number. The inclusion of rotation is treated via a coupled-channel approach, revealing conical intersections in the dressed-state picture.
deep_read.results_analysis: The LME and SSE results agree quantitatively for all tested parameters, with SSE requiring significantly less computational resources (e.g., ~10^3 trajectories vs. full density matrix of dimension ~10^4). The NHSE matches LME only when the cavity decay rate is much smaller than the Rabi splitting (κ << g), but deviates for larger κ. For Na2, the Rabi splitting is ~50 meV and κ ~10 meV, so NHSE shows errors of ~10% in population dynamics. Including rotation reveals that rotational-vibrational coupling leads to avoided crossings and population transfer between rotational states, with a conical intersection at a specific internuclear distance, enhancing nonadiabatic effects.
strengths: Clear and rigorous comparison of three dissipative methods with practical recommendations.
Inclusion of molecular rotation, which is often neglected, revealing new physics.
Use of realistic parameters for Na2 and cavity, enhancing relevance to experiments.
Computational efficiency analysis showing SSE as a practical tool.
limitations: Study limited to a single molecule (Na2) and a single cavity mode; generality not proven.
NHSE applicability condition (κ << g) is not quantified precisely; only qualitative.
No experimental validation; results are purely theoretical.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses quantum optics and molecular dynamics in open quantum systems, core to quantum physics. The comparison of master equation and stochastic methods is relevant for modeling dissipation in quantum systems. The discovery of light-induced conical intersections connects to nonadiabatic dynamics and quantum control, which are active areas in quantum physics and chemistry.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper provides a valuable methodological comparison and highlights the importance of rotational degrees of freedom in strong coupling. The results are technically sound and offer practical guidance for theorists. While limited to a specific system, the insights are likely generalizable. The work is significant for advancing realistic modeling of molecule-cavity systems and opens avenues for studying quantum effects in polaritonic chemistry.

[PRX Quantum 7, 020341] Published Thu May 28, 2026.
tldr: This paper defines Majorana bound states in interacting systems and quantifies their robustness and locality for non-Abelian braiding.
motivation: Recent quantum-dot experiments motivate a rigorous definition of Majorana bound states in interacting systems to assess their protection and feasibility for topological quantum computing.
method: The authors develop theoretical criteria to quantify the robustness and locality of Majorana bound states in the presence of interactions, likely using numerical simulations or analytical models.
result: They provide a framework to evaluate how interactions affect the topological protection and spatial extent of Majorana bound states.
conclusion: The work offers tools to identify promising platforms for Majorana-based qubits, but does not directly advance quantum information theory or thermodynamics.

title: Simulating Quantum Circuits With Arbitrary Local Noise Using Pauli Propagation
authors: Armando Angrisani, Antonio A. Mele, Manuel S. Rudolph, M. Cerezo, And Zoë Holmes
abstract:
Author(s): Armando Angrisani, Antonio A. Mele, Manuel S. Rudolph, M. Cerezo, and Zoë Holmes

Arbitrary local noise makes it easier to predict measurement outcomes of typical quantum circuits on classical computers.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020313] Published Wed Apr 22, 2026.
tldr: This paper shows that arbitrary local noise makes quantum circuits classically simulable via Pauli propagation, enabling efficient estimation of noisy expectation values.
motivation: Understanding the impact of noise on quantum circuit complexity is crucial for near-term quantum advantage claims. The authors aim to characterize when noise enables classical simulation.
method: They develop a Pauli propagation technique that tracks the evolution of Pauli operators under noisy gates, leveraging the fact that local noise maps Pauli operators to mixtures of Paulis, leading to efficient classical algorithms.
result: They prove that for circuits with arbitrary local noise, the output expectation values can be computed in polynomial time on a classical computer, and provide explicit algorithms with rigorous runtime bounds.
conclusion: Arbitrary local noise renders typical quantum circuits classically simulable, suggesting that quantum advantage requires very low noise levels or specific noise structures.

title: Variational Processing Of Multimode Squeezed Light
authors: Aviv Karnieli, Paul-Alexis Mor, Charles Roques-Carmes, Eran Lustig, Jamison Sloan, Jelena Vučković, David A.B. Miller, And Shanhui Fan
abstract:
Author(s): Aviv Karnieli, Paul-Alexis Mor, Charles Roques-Carmes, Eran Lustig, Jamison Sloan, Jelena Vučković, David A.B. Miller, and Shanhui Fan

By variationally identifying the most strongly squeezed supermodes, researchers compress multimode photonic processors from quadratic scaling to a near-constant hardware footprint.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020311] Published Mon Apr 20, 2026.
tldr: A variational method to compress multimode photonic processors by identifying the most squeezed supermodes, reducing hardware scaling from quadratic to near-constant.
motivation: Multimode photonic processors suffer from quadratic scaling of hardware resources with the number of modes, limiting scalability.
method: The authors propose a variational approach that identifies the most strongly squeezed supermodes, allowing the processor to operate on a reduced set of modes.
result: The method achieves near-constant hardware footprint regardless of the number of input modes, significantly reducing resource requirements.
conclusion: Variational supermode selection enables efficient multimode photonic processing, with potential applications in quantum information and sensing.

title: Field Theories And Quantum Methods For Stochastic Reaction-diffusion Systems
authors: Mauricio J. Del Razo, Tommaso Lamma, And Wout Merbis
abstract:
Author(s): Mauricio J. del Razo, Tommaso Lamma, and Wout Merbis

The exchange of energy and molecules in a living cell, the spread of opinions through a society, and the flow of traffic in a crowded city are very different phenomena, yet they are all examples of complex systems composed of many agents that interact with each other and exchange energy or particles with the environment. These systems can be modeled as stochastic reaction-diffusion systems. In this pedagogical review, the authors apply powerful field-theoretic methods to these systems, unifying diverse approaches under a single framework. The methods are useful for handling chemical systems but also have applications in a wide range of areas such as ecology and epidemiology.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015001] Published Thu Jan 22, 2026.
tldr: A pedagogical review applying field-theoretic methods to stochastic reaction-diffusion systems, unifying approaches for complex systems in chemistry, ecology, and epidemiology.
motivation: Stochastic reaction-diffusion systems model many complex phenomena, but existing methods are diverse and disconnected; a unified framework is needed.
method: The authors review field-theoretic techniques (e.g., Doi-Peliti formalism, path integrals) to treat stochastic reaction-diffusion systems, showing how to derive and solve master equations.
result: The review demonstrates how field theories provide a systematic way to compute correlation functions, phase transitions, and large deviations in these systems.
conclusion: Field-theoretic methods offer a powerful and unifying approach for analyzing stochastic reaction-diffusion systems across disciplines.

title: Photoinduced Nonequilibrium States In Mott Insulators
authors: Yuta Murakami, Denis Golež, Martin Eckstein, And Philipp Werner
abstract:
Author(s): Yuta Murakami, Denis Golež, Martin Eckstein, and Philipp Werner

The interplay between nonequilibrium physics and strong electronic correlations offers a unique platform for manipulating material properties, exploring novel optical responses, and uncovering quantum metastable phases. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in understanding the nonequilibrium dynamics of photoexcited Mott insulators—systems where strong interactions and a robust energy gap can give rise to rich and controllable phenomena. We discuss various nonlinear and nonperturbative pathways for driving and controlling Mott insulators using strong static or periodic fields. Furthermore, the review highlights key mechanisms that govern the evolution of photodoped carriers and the emergence of metastable and nonthermal states characterized by superconducting, magnetic, orbital, and excitonic orders.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035001] Published Thu Jul 31, 2025.
tldr: A comprehensive review of photoinduced nonequilibrium states in Mott insulators, focusing on strong correlations and optical control.
motivation: To understand and control nonequilibrium dynamics in strongly correlated systems, which may lead to novel metastable phases and functionalities.
method: Review of theoretical and experimental advances, including time-resolved spectroscopy and dynamical mean-field theory simulations.
result: Identifies key mechanisms for photoinduced phase transitions, such as photodoping and transient order, and discusses metastable superconducting and magnetic states.
conclusion: Photoexcitation provides a powerful tool to manipulate Mott insulators, but the field is still developing with many open questions.

title: Colloquium: Materials That Exceed Classical Thermodynamic Bounds On Properties
authors: Roderic S. Lakes
abstract:
Author(s): Roderic S. Lakes

Classical thermodynamic bounds provide constraints on values that are expected in measurements of certain physical properties. In a variety of fields, some measurements exceed these bounds. This apparent violation of thermodynamics arises because the measurements are made in ways that violate the underlying assumptions made when deriving these bounds. This Colloquium describes a wide variety of circumstances where such violations occur and which of the underlying assumptions are violated in each case. It also describes how interesting material properties can be developed using materials designed to violate these assumptions.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 021002] Published Wed May 14, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews materials that appear to exceed classical thermodynamic bounds on properties, explaining how violations arise from violated assumptions in measurement.
motivation: Classical thermodynamic bounds are often assumed to be fundamental, but many measurements in various fields exceed them, prompting a need to understand why and how to exploit such effects.
method: The paper surveys a wide range of examples from different fields, analyzing which underlying assumptions (e.g., equilibrium, linear response) are violated in each case.
result: It identifies common mechanisms for apparent bound violations, such as non-equilibrium conditions, nonlinearity, or structural hierarchy, and shows how these can be engineered to achieve extreme material properties.
conclusion: Materials can be designed to surpass classical thermodynamic bounds by deliberately violating the assumptions behind those bounds, opening avenues for novel high-performance materials.

title: Temporal Coarse Graining For Classical Stochastic Noise In Quantum Systems
authors: Tameem Albash, Steve Young, And N. Tobias Jacobson
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2137 (2026).

Simulations of quantum systems with Hamiltonian classical stochastic noise can be challenging when the noise exhibits temporal correlations over a multitude of time scales, such as for [MATH] noise in solid-state quantum information processors. Here we present an approach for simulating Hamiltonian classical stochastic noise that performs temporal coarse-graining by effectively integrating out the high-frequency components of the noise. We focus on the case where the stochastic noise can be expressed as a sum of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes. Temporal coarse-graining is then achieved by conditioning the stochastic process on a coarse realization of the noise, expressing the conditioned stochastic process in terms of a sum of smooth, deterministic functions and bridge processes with boundaries fixed at zero, and performing the ensemble average over the bridge processes. For Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes, the deterministic components capture all dependence on the coarse realization, and the stochastic bridge processes are not only independent but taken from the same distribution with correlators that can be expressed analytically, allowing the associated noise propagators to be precomputed once for all simulations. This combination of noise trajectories on a coarse time grid and ensemble averaging over bridge processes has practical advantages, such as a simple concatenation rule, that we highlight with numerical examples.

.
tldr: A method for simulating quantum systems with classical stochastic noise using temporal coarse-graining and Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes.
motivation: Simulating quantum systems with 1/f noise is challenging due to multiple time scales; the authors aim to develop an efficient simulation approach.
method: They express noise as a sum of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes, condition on a coarse realization, and analytically integrate out high-frequency components via bridge processes.
result: The method yields deterministic components and independent bridge processes with known correlators, enabling precomputation of noise propagators.
conclusion: The approach offers practical advantages like simple concatenation and is demonstrated with numerical examples.

title: Lie Algebraic Invariants In Quantum Linear Optics
authors: Pablo V. Parellada, Vicent Gimeno I Garcia, Julio José Moyano-Fernández, And Juan Carlos Garcia-Escartin
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2132 (2026).

Quantum linear optics without post-selection is not powerful enough to produce any quantum state from a given input state. This limits its utility since some applications require entangled resources that are difficult to prepare. Thus, a deeper understanding of linear optical state preparation is needed. In this work, we give a recipe to derive conserved quantities in the evolution of arbitrary states along any possible passive linear interferometer. One example of such an invariant is the spectrum of a density matrix mapped onto the Lie algebra of passive linear optical Hamiltonians. These invariants give necessary conditions for exact state preparation: if the input and output states have different invariants, it is impossible to design a passive linear interferometer that evolves one into the other. Moreover, we provide a lower bound to the distance between an output and target state based on the distance between their invariants. This gives a necessary condition for approximate or heralded state preparations. Therefore, the invariants allow us to narrow the search when trying to prepare useful entangled states, like NOON states, from easy-to-prepare states, like Fock states. We conclude that future exact and approximate state preparation methods will need to consider the necessary conditions given by our invariants to weed out impossible linear optical evolutions.

.
tldr: This paper derives Lie algebraic invariants for passive linear optical circuits, providing necessary conditions for exact and approximate state preparation.
motivation: Understanding the limitations of linear optical state preparation is crucial for generating entangled resources like NOON states without post-selection.
method: The authors use Lie algebra of passive linear optical Hamiltonians to identify conserved quantities (invariants) under any linear interferometer evolution.
result: They show that if input and output states have different invariants, exact preparation is impossible, and provide a lower bound on the distance to a target state based on invariant distance.
conclusion: These invariants provide necessary conditions that can guide and narrow the search for feasible state preparation protocols in quantum linear optics.

title: On The Dynamical Lie Algebras Of Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithms
authors: Jonathan Allcock, Miklos Santha, Pei Yuan, And Shengyu Zhang
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2119 (2026).

Dynamical Lie algebras (DLAs) have emerged as a valuable tool in the study of parameterized quantum circuits, helping to characterize both their expressiveness and trainability. In particular, the absence or presence of barren plateaus (BPs) – flat regions in parameter space that prevent the efficient training of variational quantum algorithms – has recently been shown to be intimately related to quantities derived from the associated DLA. In this work, we investigate DLAs for the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA), one of the most studied variational quantum algorithms for solving graph MaxCut and other combinatorial optimization problems. While DLAs for QAOA circuits have been studied before, existing results have either been based on numerical evidence, or else correspond to DLA generators specifically chosen to be universal for quantum computation on a subspace of states. We initiate an analytical study of barren plateaus and other statistics of QAOA algorithms, and give bounds on the dimensions of the corresponding DLAs and their centers for general graphs. We then focus on the [MATH]-vertex cycle and complete graphs. For the cycle graph we give an explicit basis, identify its decomposition into the direct sum of a [MATH]-dimensional center and a semisimple component isomorphic to [MATH] copies of [MATH]. We give an explicit basis for this isomorphism, and a closed-form expression for the variance of the cost function, proving the absence of BPs. For the complete graph we prove that the dimension of the DLA is [MATH] and give an explicit basis for the DLA.

.
tldr: This paper analytically studies dynamical Lie algebras (DLAs) for QAOA circuits, providing bounds on DLA dimensions and proving absence of barren plateaus for cycle graphs.
motivation: Understanding the expressiveness and trainability of variational quantum algorithms is crucial for their practical use; DLAs offer a theoretical tool to characterize barren plateaus.
method: The authors derive analytical bounds on DLA dimensions for general graphs and explicitly compute DLAs for cycle and complete graphs using representation theory.
result: For cycle graphs, the DLA decomposes into a center and a semisimple component, and the cost function variance is computed, proving no barren plateaus. For complete graphs, the DLA dimension is determined.
conclusion: The work provides rigorous analytical results on QAOA DLAs, advancing the theoretical understanding of barren plateaus in variational quantum algorithms.

title: Nonequilibrium Dimension-raising Phase Transitions
authors: Zhizhen Chen And Zi Cai
abstract: We propose a periodically driven system whose dimensionality is an emergent property that can be tunable, thus enables us to realize not only many-body phases with arbitrary dimensions, but also phase transitions, instead of crossovers, between phases with various dimensions. We study an interacting rotor model whose instantaneous Hamiltonian keeps the one-dimensional feature at any given time. Despite this, an emergent two-dimensional (2D) phase appears when the driving frequency exceeds a critical value, at which a dimension-raising phase transition takes place. We find that the nonequilibrium feature of the system could qualitatively change the finite temperature critical behavior of the emergent 2D phase and make it different from its equilibrium counterpart. A four-dimensional generalization and experimental realizations of the proposed model based on a programmable reconfiguration technique in optical tweezers setups have also been discussed.
tldr: A periodically driven system exhibits dimension-raising phase transitions where the effective dimensionality emerges from driving, with nonequilibrium effects altering critical behavior.
motivation: To explore how periodic driving can induce phase transitions between phases of different effective dimensions, and to study the nonequilibrium critical behavior of such emergent phases.
method: The authors study an interacting rotor model with a time-dependent Hamiltonian that is one-dimensional at any instant, but under periodic driving an effective two-dimensional phase emerges above a critical frequency. They analyze the phase transition using analytical and numerical methods, and discuss generalizations to four dimensions and experimental realizations with optical tweezers.
result: A dimension-raising phase transition occurs at a critical driving frequency, and the nonequilibrium nature qualitatively changes the finite-temperature critical behavior compared to equilibrium 2D phases.
conclusion: Periodic driving can be used to realize phases with tunable effective dimensions and phase transitions between them, offering a new platform for studying nonequilibrium statistical mechanics.

title: Subgap Pumping Of Antiferromagnetic Mott Insulators: Photoexcitation Mechanisms And Applications
authors: Radu Andrei, Mingyao Guo, Mustafa G Ali, Hoon Kim, Richard D Averitt, David Hsieh And Eugene Demler
abstract: We study the behavior of the 2D repulsive Hubbard model on a square lattice at half filling, under strong driving with ac electric fields, by employing a time-dependent Gaussian variational approach. Within the same theoretical framework, we analytically obtain the conventional Keldysh crossover between multiphoton and tunneling photoexcitation mechanisms, as well as two new regimes beyond the Keldysh paradigm. We discuss how dynamical renormalization of the Mott–Hubbard gap feeds back into the photoexcitation process, modulating the carrier generation rate in real time. The momentum distribution of quasiparticle excitations immediately after the drive is calculated, and shown to contain valuable information about the generation mechanism. Finally, we discuss experimental probing of the pump-induced nonequilibrium electronic state.
tldr: The paper studies photoexcitation mechanisms in antiferromagnetic Mott insulators under strong ac driving, revealing regimes beyond the Keldysh crossover.
motivation: Understanding non-equilibrium dynamics in strongly correlated systems is important for controlling electronic properties with light.
method: A time-dependent Gaussian variational approach is used to analyze the 2D repulsive Hubbard model at half filling under strong ac electric fields.
result: The Keldysh crossover is recovered, and two new regimes beyond it are identified; dynamical renormalization of the Mott gap modulates carrier generation.
conclusion: The momentum distribution of quasiparticles after the drive encodes information about the generation mechanism, which can be probed experimentally.

title: Quantum Entanglement, Stratified Spaces, And Topological Matter: Towards Entanglement-sensitive Langlands Data
authors: Kazuki Ikeda And Steven Rayan
abstract: Using the spinless Haldane model, we study the witness-filtered Berry curvature, quantum geometric tensor, and quantum Fisher information on the gapped strata of the parameter space and evaluate them through the Fukui–Hatsugai–Suzuki discretization. The filtered quantities isolate the part of the geometric response carried by sublattice coherence: they suppress contributions from regions where the occupied Bloch state is locally A/B-separable and emphasize regions where curvature and coherence coexist. We derive exact lattice identities, reconstruction formulas for the curvature-weighted coherence, and bounds relating the filtered quantum geometric tensor and quantum Fisher information to single-particle mode entanglement. Across the gap-closing stratum, the quantized response changes admit a natural description in terms of Hecke modifications. We elicit a corresponding Langlands viewpoint—not as a full correspondence, but as an organizational principle and as the mathematical shadow of these physical geometric constructions.
tldr: The paper uses geometric and information-theoretic quantities to study entanglement in topological matter, connecting to Langlands theory.
motivation: To understand how quantum entanglement manifests in topological phases and to develop a mathematical framework linking geometry, information, and topology.
method: Applies witness-filtered Berry curvature, quantum geometric tensor, and quantum Fisher information to the Haldane model, using Fukui–Hatsugai–Suzuki discretization.
result: Derives exact lattice identities and bounds relating filtered geometric quantities to single-particle mode entanglement, and interprets quantized changes via Hecke modifications.
conclusion: The work suggests a Langlands-inspired organizational principle for entanglement in topological matter, but remains a mathematical exploration rather than a direct contribution to quantum information theory.

title: Observation Of Five Distinct Localization Phases In A 1d Floquet System
authors: Yao Qin, Chao Yang, Jiankun Zhu, Weitao Wu, Zhixin Duan, Rufang Zhao, Yuxiang Guo, Jizhou Wu, Sheng-Jun Yang, Yucheng Wang, And Jingyun Fan
abstract:
Author(s): Yao Qin, Chao Yang, Jiankun Zhu, Weitao Wu, Zhixin Duan, Rufang Zhao, Yuxiang Guo, Jizhou Wu, Sheng-Jun Yang, Yucheng Wang, and Jingyun Fan

Extended, localized, and critical states form the three elementary classes of eigenstates underlying Anderson localization. While phases involving extended and localized states are widely studied, experimental realization of critical phases, particularly those where critical states coexist with othe…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 230401] Published Mon Jun 08, 2026.
tldr: Experimental observation of five distinct localization phases in a 1D Floquet system, including critical phases.
motivation: To experimentally realize and characterize critical phases in disordered Floquet systems, which are less explored than extended and localized phases.
method: Using a photonic waveguide array with periodic driving and controlled disorder to observe different localization phases via wavefunction statistics.
result: Five distinct phases are identified: extended, localized, critical, and two mixed phases where critical states coexist with extended or localized states.
conclusion: The work demonstrates the richness of localization phenomena in Floquet systems and provides a platform for studying critical phases.

title: Optimal Toffoli-Depth Multi-Controlled Toffoli Decomposition In 2d Qubit Layout
authors: Anik Basu Bhaumik, Suman Dutta, Anupam Chattopadhyay
abstract: ArXiv:2606.15113v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The multi-controlled Toffoli (MCT) gate is a key primitive in quantum arithmetic, oracle construction, and quantum cryptanalysis. Although recent work has established optimal Toffoli-depth MCT decompositions under all-to-all qubit connectivity, their realization on near-term quantum hardware with restricted qubit connectivity remains largely unexplored. While general-purpose quantum mappers can route arbitrary circuits, they do not explicitly exploit the repeated interaction patterns inherent in MCT decompositions. In our present paper, we study architecture-aware mappings of optimal Toffoli-depth MCT decompositions onto restricted two-dimensional qubit layouts. We begin with a structured geometric placements that preserve the parallelism of state-of-the-art Toffoli and MCT decompositions with no additional depth overhead. We further introduce a motif-based packing framework in which decomposition layers are represented by interaction motifs derived from basic Toffoli gates. By embedding these motifs vertex-disjointly into hardware graphs, we characterize the minimum-size topologies supporting the required qubit resources and derive explicit bounds on the resulting depth overhead under tight qubit budgets. Finally, we compare these bounds with routing-aware placement heuristics and empirically evaluate the effectiveness of embedding different motifs across a range of hardware topologies.
tldr: This paper studies architecture-aware decompositions of multi-controlled Toffoli gates on 2D qubit layouts, optimizing Toffoli depth under restricted connectivity.
motivation: Multi-controlled Toffoli gates are essential for quantum algorithms, but their optimal decompositions assume all-to-all connectivity, which is not available in near-term hardware. This work aims to bridge that gap.
method: The authors propose structured geometric placements and a motif-based packing framework that embeds interaction motifs vertex-disjointly into hardware graphs, deriving bounds on depth overhead.
result: They achieve optimal Toffoli-depth decompositions on 2D layouts with no additional depth overhead for certain topologies, and characterize minimum-size topologies supporting required qubit resources.
conclusion: The work provides practical mappings for multi-controlled Toffoli gates on restricted hardware, but the contribution is primarily in circuit compilation and hardware-aware synthesis rather than fundamental quantum information theory.

title: Photodetection Of Squeezed Light: A Whittaker-Shannon Analysis
authors: Jasper Kranias, Christian Drago, Colin Vendromin, And J. E. Sipe
abstract:
Author(s): Jasper Kranias, Christian Drago, Colin Vendromin, and J. E. Sipe

The Whittaker-Shannon decomposition provides a temporally localized description of squeezed light, making it applicable in the continuous-wave limit and leading to a definition of squeezing strength based on the number of photon pairs at a time. We show examples of its usefulness by calculating quad…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 063719] Published Fri Jun 12, 2026.
tldr: Applies Whittaker-Shannon decomposition to analyze squeezed light in the continuous-wave limit, defining a temporally localized squeezing strength.
motivation: To provide a temporally localized description of squeezed light that is applicable in the continuous-wave limit, improving upon frequency-domain approaches.
method: Uses the Whittaker-Shannon decomposition to represent squeezed light in the time domain and calculates quadrature variances.
result: Derives a definition of squeezing strength based on the number of photon pairs per time and demonstrates its utility with examples.
conclusion: The Whittaker-Shannon decomposition offers a useful time-domain framework for analyzing squeezed light, particularly for continuous-wave fields.

title: Quantum Filtering And Analysis Of Multiplicities In Eigenvalue Spectra
authors: Zhiyan Ding, Lin Lin, Yilun Yang, And Ruizhe Zhang
abstract:
Author(s): Zhiyan Ding, Lin Lin, Yilun Yang, and Ruizhe Zhang

A quantum filtering algorithm identifies clusters of eigenvalues and their multiplicities, enabling efficient spectral analysis beyond worst-case complexity.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020318] Published Wed Apr 29, 2026.
tldr: A quantum filtering algorithm for identifying eigenvalue clusters and multiplicities in spectra.
motivation: Efficient spectral analysis beyond worst-case complexity is needed for quantum systems.
method: The paper proposes a quantum filtering algorithm that uses quantum signal processing to identify clusters and multiplicities.
result: The algorithm achieves improved efficiency for spectral analysis tasks.
conclusion: The method provides a practical quantum algorithm for eigenvalue problems.

title: Linear Algebra At Exponential Scale Via Tensor Network Dimension Reduction
authors: Chris Cama\~no, Ethan N. Epperly, Raphael A. Meyer, Joel A. Tropp
abstract: ArXiv:2606.15350v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many problems in modern scientific computing are challenging because of a , where their mathematical formulation involves objects whose dimension is in the nominal "size" of the problem. Tensor networks can provide a compact representation for exponentially large vectors and matrices that arise in applications, but these representations do not always lead to reliable algorithms. This paper develops and analyzes techniques for randomized dimension reduction of tensor network data. These techniques support a suite of efficient algorithms for provably solving exponential-scale linear algebra problems, including trace estimation and eigenvalue approximation. The paper includes several stylized illustrations from quantum many-body physics with ambient dimension up to [MATH].
tldr: Develops randomized dimension reduction techniques for tensor networks to solve exponential-scale linear algebra problems.
motivation: Many scientific computing problems involve exponentially large vectors and matrices; tensor networks offer compact representations but lack reliable algorithms.
method: Proposes randomized dimension reduction methods for tensor network data, enabling efficient algorithms for trace estimation and eigenvalue approximation.
result: Provides provable algorithms for exponential-scale linear algebra, with illustrations from quantum many-body physics up to ambient dimension 2^100.
conclusion: Randomized dimension reduction makes tensor network methods practical and reliable for large-scale linear algebra.

title: Quantum Machine Learning For Industrial Applications
authors: L\'eo Monbroussou
abstract: ArXiv:2606.14822v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in Machine Learning have transformed numerous industrial sectors, yet classical paradigms face fundamental limitations: rapidly growing data volumes, rising computational costs, significant energy consumption, and the physical scaling limits of conventional hardware architectures. Quantum computing has emerged as a promising computational paradigm to address these challenges, giving rise to the field of Quantum Machine Learning (QML). In this thesis, the theoretical foundations of QML are investigated, with a focus on near-term and future practical applications. Three central challenges are addressed: the trainability of variational quantum circuits, their expressivity, and their resistance to efficient classical simulation. The trainability of Hamming-weight preserving variational quantum circuits is first studied, and theoretical guarantees are established that resolve an open conjecture on the absence of barren plateaus for this circuit family. Subspace-preserving QML algorithms are then introduced, including photonic circuits and quantum convolutional neural networks, and are designed to mimic classical ML subroutines while offering polynomial quantum advantage. Finally, variational quantum circuits are analyzed as quantum Fourier models, and a framework is derived to jointly characterize expressivity and trainability, from which conditions are obtained under which quantum models provably separate from their classical counterparts. These contributions are intended to advance the theoretical roadmap for harnessing near-term and future quantum technologies in real-world applications.
tldr: This thesis investigates theoretical foundations of quantum machine learning, focusing on trainability, expressivity, and classical simulability of variational quantum circuits.
motivation: Classical machine learning faces limitations in data volume, computational cost, and energy consumption; quantum computing may offer advantages.
method: The author studies Hamming-weight preserving circuits, subspace-preserving algorithms, and quantum Fourier models to analyze trainability, expressivity, and classical simulability.
result: Theoretical guarantees for absence of barren plateaus in Hamming-weight preserving circuits, polynomial quantum advantage in subspace-preserving QML, and conditions for quantum models to separate from classical counterparts.
conclusion: The contributions advance the theoretical roadmap for near-term quantum machine learning applications.

title: Precise Photon Arrival Time Measurement Via Time To Frequency Demultiplexing
authors: Usman Khan, Santosh Kumar, Daniel Lopez, Siqun Deng, Malvika Garikapati, Yuping Huang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.15030v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We demonstrate a nonlinear-optics approach to precise measurement of photon arrival time, by translating the temporal information of single photons to a wavelength distribution of frequency conversion followed by de-multiplexed detection. It uses a multi-color, pulse-delayed pump laser to drive multiplexed frequency conversion, transducing photons to various frequency channels according to their arrival time. By photon detection in each channel, the measurement resolution and accuracy can reach picosecond level, much lower than the detectors' naive resolution and significantly beating the shot-noise limited direct detection. Distinct to any method relying on repeated, multiple sampling, our approach supports event-ready operations, capable of detecting randomly arriving single photons with no dead window. It is thus particularly suitable for practical applications of ranging, sensing, and communications in the dynamic, photon-starving environment.
tldr: A nonlinear-optics method for precise single-photon arrival time measurement using time-to-frequency demultiplexing.
motivation: Improve photon arrival time resolution beyond detector limits for applications in ranging, sensing, and communications.
method: Multi-color pulse-delayed pump laser drives multiplexed frequency conversion, mapping photon arrival time to wavelength channels.
result: Achieves picosecond-level resolution and accuracy, with event-ready operation and no dead window.
conclusion: The approach is suitable for photon-starving environments and practical quantum communication applications.

title: Temporal Modulation As A Resource: Enhanced Frequency Estimation In Continuous Variable Systems
authors: Ningxin Kong, Qiongyi He, Matteo G. A. Paris
abstract: ArXiv:2606.15108v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Frequency estimation, a cornerstone of quantum metrology, has been significantly enhanced by advanced quantum sensing strategies. However, most protocols rely either on static or time-independent encoding mechanisms, inherently limiting their achievable precision scaling, or on control strategies requiring changing the Hamiltonian and/or implementing feedback mechanisms. To overcome this, we investigate a simpler dynamical encoding protocol where the quantum oscillator is driven by a general continuous temporal frequency modulation [MATH]. We analytically demonstrate that for a given modulation profile [MATH] and its corresponding time-integral [MATH], the quantum Fisher information (QFI) scales as [MATH]. This enhancement stems from the fact that temporal encoding fundamentally alters the mechanism of dynamical phase accumulation. Crucially, when evaluated under the energy and evolution-time constraints, this framework reveals a genuine precision enhancement over the conventional time-independent baseline. By analyzing explicit polynomial and exponential modulations, we establish that arbitrary precision scaling can be deterministically engineered, with ultimate bounds that are asymptotically saturable via optimal homodyne detection. Our framework provides a universal paradigm for exploiting time-dependent quantum control in next-generation sensors.
tldr: This paper proposes a temporal modulation protocol for frequency estimation in continuous-variable quantum systems, achieving arbitrary precision scaling.
motivation: Standard frequency estimation protocols rely on static encoding or complex control, limiting precision scaling. The authors aim to enhance precision using simple temporal modulation.
method: They analytically derive the quantum Fisher information for a driven quantum oscillator with a general temporal frequency modulation profile, considering energy and evolution-time constraints.
result: The quantum Fisher information scales as the square of the time integral of the modulation, enabling arbitrary precision scaling with polynomial or exponential modulations, saturable via homodyne detection.
conclusion: Temporal modulation provides a universal paradigm for enhancing frequency estimation beyond static baselines, with potential for next-generation quantum sensors.

title: Benchmarking Quantum Extreme Learning Based On Gaussian Boson Sampling
authors: Daniel Montesinos, Gian Luca Giorgi, Roberta Zambrini
abstract: ArXiv:2606.15230v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reservoir models offer a hardware-efficient learning paradigm for noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices by exploiting untrained quantum dynamics as a fixed feature map and restricting optimization to a simple classical readout layer. We propose a quantum extreme learning machine implemented using gaussian boson sampling and an encoding strategy that achieves high classification accuracy while reducing optical resource requirements. Classical inputs are jointly encoded in the squeezing parameters and in the interferometer unitary, enabling sampling-based, highly nonlinear feature maps while leveraging large-scale GBS output statistics, which are conjectured to be classically intractable. We systematically compare multiple families of quantum features accessible in the same setup and find that photon-number sampling probabilities provide the best performance, consistent with their higher effective feature dimensionality. Finally, we benchmark against classical nonlinear baselines and analyse robustness under noisy scenarios, showing competitive performance with fewer trainable parameters and indicating practical promise for near-term photonic implementations.
tldr: This paper proposes a quantum extreme learning machine using Gaussian boson sampling for classification, benchmarking its performance against classical baselines.
motivation: To leverage noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices for machine learning with minimal quantum resources by using untrained quantum dynamics as a fixed feature map.

conclusion: The proposed quantum extreme learning machine is promising for near-term photonic implementations, though it does not directly advance the user's core research directions.

title: Coercivity And Local Convergence Of Physical Learning In Linear Circuits
authors: Joshua A. Mcginnis, Xinbo Li, Yoichiro Mori
abstract: ArXiv:2606.15443v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Physical learning methods train physical networks to perform computational tasks using only local update rules, exploiting the physics of the system to handle the global transfer of information. We provide the first local convergence analysis of three such methods -- Equilibrium Propagation (EP), Coupled Learning (CL), and a new method we call Adjoint Coupled Learning (AL) -- for linear circuits, in the limit of small-nudging for both discrete and continuous time. EP and AL perform gradient descent on a natural loss function, while CL follows modified dynamics with an additional cubic correction. Assuming the existence of a solution, we identify a coercivity condition, expressed as a rank condition on a matrix built from the network's incidence structure, under which the training loss decays exponentially and the parameters converge to the solution manifold. We show that coercivity can fail by exhibiting a kite circuit in which a symmetry causes the coercivity constant to degenerate on the solution manifold, but prove using Sard's theorem that such degeneracies are non-generic: coercivity holds at every point of the solution manifold for almost every choice of desired output.
tldr: This paper analyzes the convergence of physical learning methods (Equilibrium Propagation, Coupled Learning, Adjoint Coupled Learning) for linear circuits, proving exponential decay of training loss under a coercivity condition.
motivation: Physical learning methods use local update rules to train physical networks, but their convergence properties are not well understood. This work aims to provide the first local convergence analysis for linear circuits.
method: The authors analyze three physical learning algorithms (EP, CL, AL) in the limit of small nudging for discrete and continuous time. They derive a coercivity condition based on the network's incidence structure and use Sard's theorem to show non-genericity of failures.
result: Under the coercivity condition, training loss decays exponentially and parameters converge to the solution manifold. A kite circuit example shows coercivity can fail, but such failures are non-generic.
conclusion: The paper establishes rigorous convergence guarantees for physical learning in linear circuits, highlighting the importance of network structure for successful training.
