Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Volume 123, Issue 23, June 2026.
SignificanceTwo-sample testing examines whether two probability distributions on some feature space differ based on random samples. It is fundamental in statistics and machine learning, especially when feature spaces are complex. Such settings are ...
tldr: This paper uses kernel embeddings to study the separation of measures phenomenon in two-sample testing.
motivation: Two-sample testing is fundamental in statistics and machine learning, especially for complex feature spaces.
method: The authors employ kernel embeddings and analyze the separation of measures to develop new testing procedures.
result: The paper presents theoretical results on the separation of measures and demonstrates improved testing performance.
conclusion: Kernel embeddings provide a powerful framework for two-sample testing, with implications for statistical inference.

title: Layerwise Stratification And Band Reordering In Twisted Multilayer MoTe2
authors: Yueyao Fanxiao-Wei Zhangyusen Yexiaoyu Liuchong Wangkaijie Yangdi Xiaoting Caoahttps://ror.org/00cvxb145department Of Materials Science And Engineering, University Of Washington, Seattle, WA 98195bhttps://ror.org/00cvxb145department Of Physics, University Of Washington, Seattle, WA 98195
abstract:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Volume 123, Issue 23, June 2026.
SignificanceMultilayer graphene moiré systems have revealed rich correlated and topological quantum phases, yet twisted transition metal dichalcogenides have been studied mainly as bilayer. Here we show that adding more layers changes the underlying ...
tldr: This paper studies layerwise stratification and band reordering in twisted multilayer MoTe2, a condensed matter physics topic on moiré systems.
motivation: To understand how adding more layers changes the electronic structure and correlated phases in twisted transition metal dichalcogenides, which have been studied mainly as bilayers.
method: The authors likely use first-principles calculations or tight-binding models to analyze the band structure and layer-dependent properties of twisted multilayer MoTe2.
result: They find that increasing the number of layers leads to significant band reordering and stratification effects, altering the moiré potential and correlated phases.
conclusion: Multilayer twisted TMDs exhibit richer physics than bilayers, and layer number is a crucial tuning parameter for engineering quantum phases.

title: Ultrafast Terahertz And Optical Spectroscopy Under Synergetic Extreme Conditions
authors: Xinbo Wang, Tao Dong, Jianlin Luo, Nanlin Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.14726v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Elucidating and manipulating emergent phases in complex materials requires direct access to their low-energy collective modes. Terahertz (THz) time-domain and ultrafast optical spectroscopies have emerged as indispensable experimental tools, enabling the probing of intrinsic electrodynamics and the coherent control of non-equilibrium states. At the Synergetic Extreme Condition User Facility (SECUF), we have developed a suite of intense ultrashort light sources covering the near-infrared, mid-infrared, and THz spectral ranges. By integrating these strong-field pulses with extreme sample environments, such as low temperatures, strong magnetic fields, and high pressures, we have established several state-of-the-art spectroscopy platforms. In this article, we outline the technical specifications of each setup and highlight representative user experiments. The presented results underscore the exceptional capability of the THz experimental unit (A4-2) to explore ultrafast dynamics across a multi-parameter thermodynamic phase space.
tldr: This paper describes the development of ultrafast terahertz and optical spectroscopy platforms at a user facility for studying emergent phases in complex materials under extreme conditions.
motivation: To understand and manipulate emergent phases in complex materials, direct access to low-energy collective modes is needed, which requires advanced spectroscopy under extreme conditions.
method: The authors developed intense ultrashort light sources covering near-infrared to THz ranges and integrated them with low-temperature, high-magnetic-field, and high-pressure sample environments at the Synergetic Extreme Condition User Facility.
result: They established several state-of-the-art spectroscopy platforms and demonstrated their capability through representative user experiments, highlighting the THz experimental unit's performance.
conclusion: The developed platforms enable exploration of ultrafast dynamics across a multi-parameter thermodynamic phase space, providing a powerful tool for materials research.

title: A Reverse Hard-Core Model In $\mathbb{A}_2$: An Application Of The Pirogov-Sinai Theory
authors: A. Mazel, I. Stuhl, Y. Suhov
abstract: ArXiv:2606.14903v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper we use the Pirogov--Sinai theory to analyze a class of particle models of Statistical Mechanics on the unit triangular lattice [MATH]. The models are specified by two parameters: the particle activity [MATH] and a positive L\"oschian number [MATH] interpreted as a maximal squared clearing radius. Admissible configurations are those in which every empty lattice site has an occupied site within squared distance at most [MATH], thereby forbidding empty disks of radius exceeding or equal [MATH]. The Hamiltonian favors configurations with as few occupied sites as possible, while the admissibility condition enforces a positive density of particles. We prove that the periodic ground states of the model, i.e., the configurations achieving an optimal balance of two tendencies, are the ones whose occupied sites form triangular sublattices of explicitly determined squared side-length [MATH]. Furthermore, for sufficiently small values of the activity parameter [MATH], some (but not necessarily all) periodic ground states generate extreme Gibbs (DLR) measures. We describe the resulting phase structure and characterize the pure phases associated with stable ground states.
tldr: This paper uses Pirogov-Sinai theory to analyze a hard-core lattice gas model on the triangular lattice, focusing on ground states and phase structure.
motivation: To understand the equilibrium phases of a statistical mechanics model with a constraint forbidding large empty disks, which is a classical problem in rigorous statistical mechanics.
method: The authors apply Pirogov-Sinai theory to classify periodic ground states and prove existence of Gibbs measures for small activities.
result: Periodic ground states are triangular sublattices with explicit side lengths, and for small activity some of these ground states yield extreme Gibbs measures.
conclusion: The model exhibits a phase diagram with multiple stable phases, characterized by the Pirogov-Sinai theory.

title: Structure-Informed Neural Operators For Long-Time Prediction Of Parametric Hamiltonian PDEs
authors: Victory C. Obieke, Christopher Chukwuemeka, Emmanuel E. Oguadimma
abstract: ArXiv:2606.14913v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hamiltonian partial differential equations (PDEs) often exhibit long-time dynamics governed by conserved quantities such as mass, momentum, and Hamiltonian energy. Standard Fourier neural operators (FNOs) provide efficient data-driven approximations of solution operators, but may not preserve these invariants during autoregressive rollout, and can develop drift in conserved quantities, phase error, and loss of qualitative accuracy. We propose an energy-projection Fourier neural operator (EP-FNO), a structure-informed operator learning architecture that combines a residual FNO time-stepping update with an invariant projection for long-time prediction of parametric Hamiltonian PDEs. We also provide a theoretical analysis showing that EP-FNO can approximate operators associated with PDEs efficiently, we also suggest a stability estimate. We evaluate the approach on the Zakharov--Kuznetsov, Kadomtsev--Petviashvili, and sine--Gordon equations. Numerical experiments show that the projected model improves long-time stability, and gives more accurate propagation of soliton and coherent wave structures compared with a standard FNO baseline. Our results demonstrate that invariant projection improves the reliability of learned surrogates for long-time Hamiltonian PDE simulation.
tldr: This paper proposes a structure-informed neural operator for long-time prediction of Hamiltonian PDEs, focusing on preserving conserved quantities.
motivation: Standard Fourier neural operators fail to preserve invariants like energy during long-time autoregressive rollout, leading to drift and phase errors.
method: The authors combine a residual FNO time-stepping update with an invariant projection step to enforce conservation laws, and provide theoretical approximation and stability analysis.
result: Numerical experiments on Zakharov–Kuznetsov, Kadomtsev–Petviashvili, and sine–Gordon equations show improved long-time stability and accuracy compared to standard FNO.
conclusion: Invariant projection enhances the reliability of learned surrogates for long-time simulation of Hamiltonian PDEs.

title: Patterns In A Warming Ocean: Stylized Spectral Facts On Sea Surface Temperature
authors: Roberto Da Silvaa, Eliseu Venites Filho, Eduardo V. Stock, Sebastian Goncalves
abstract: ArXiv:2606.14916v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Capturing stylized facts and their evolution is essential for understanding the impact of climate change on complex environmental systems. In this work, we investigate the spectral properties of correlation matrices constructed from sea surface temperature data, employing tools from random matrix theory to identify signatures of global warming and long-term climate variability. By constructing yearly ensembles of correlation matrices, we analyze the evolution of both the eigenvalue density and the statistical behavior of the largest eigenvalue. Our results reveal significant departures from the universal behavior expected for random correlations. In particular, the empirical spectra systematically deviate from the Marchenko--Pastur law, indicating the presence of strong collective correlations in ocean temperature dynamics. Moreover, we find that the average largest eigenvalue exhibits a pronounced increase over time, closely following the rise in global mean ocean temperature. The distribution of the largest eigenvalue is found to be approximately Gaussian rather than Tracy--Widom, suggesting that the system lies outside the standard universal regime associated with weakly correlated Wishart ensembles. Together with conventional statistical indicators, these spectral signatures consistently reflect the progressive modification of the ocean-temperature correlation structure. Our findings demonstrate that spectral observables derived from correlation matrices, particularly the largest eigenvalue and its fluctuations, provide a sensitive framework for characterizing climate dynamics and detecting emerging signatures of long-term climate change.
tldr: Applies random matrix theory to sea surface temperature data to detect climate change signatures.
motivation: To understand how global warming modifies ocean temperature correlation structures using spectral methods.
method: Constructs yearly correlation matrices from SST data and analyzes eigenvalue distributions, comparing to Marchenko-Pastur and Tracy-Widom laws.
result: Empirical spectra deviate from random matrix predictions; largest eigenvalue increases with global temperature and follows a Gaussian distribution.
conclusion: Spectral observables from correlation matrices are sensitive indicators of long-term climate change.

title: Dynamic Doppler Effects On Dirac Spinor Fields
authors: Alex Mahalov Bryce M. Barclay
abstract: ArXiv:2606.14952v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We derive the dynamic Doppler effects of noninertial observer motion on Dirac spinor fields, characterizing how proper acceleration, proper jerk, observer path curvature, torsion, and hyper-torsion modify the inertial quantum description of free particles. We quantify the nonlinear behavior of the amplitude and phase of the Dirac spinor wave field and isolate the spin-induced signatures that have no counterpart in the scalar Klein-Gordon field. For worldlines with constant proper jerk the amplitude scales super-exponentially as [MATH]. The complex Frenet-Serret curvature invariants generate both an exponential amplitude factor and a spin-induced phase factor. Spinor structure therefore produces an observable dynamic Doppler signature distinct from any scalar prediction.
tldr: The paper derives dynamic Doppler effects for Dirac spinor fields under noninertial motion, showing spin-induced signatures beyond scalar fields.
motivation: To understand how noninertial observer motion modifies the quantum description of Dirac particles, particularly spinor field behavior.
method: Analytical derivation using Frenet-Serret formalism and proper acceleration, jerk, curvature, torsion, and hypertorsion.
result: Proper jerk leads to super-exponential amplitude scaling; spinor structure produces observable dynamic Doppler signatures distinct from scalar predictions.
conclusion: Noninertial motion induces unique spin-dependent effects in Dirac fields that could be experimentally tested.

title: Atom Optics For Multidimensional Raman Interferometry
authors: Yingpeng Zhao, Yiyang Shao, Wenjian Tong, Shuning Bao, Yuanlong Zhang, Mengnan Yi, Shengzhe Wang, Ke Shen, Bin Wu, Yanying Feng
abstract: ArXiv:2606.15215v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The coherent control of atomic wave packets in multiple momentum dimensions is a central challenge in Raman atom optics and a key requirement for multidimensional atom interferometry. In this paper, a momentum-basis theoretical framework is developed for two-dimensional Raman interactions. We formulate the atom-laser interaction for two-dimensional Raman beams and obtain the effective two-level ground-state Hamiltonian after adiabatic elimination of the excited states. The resulted Hamiltonian is constructed on the reachable momentum-state lattice and includes AC Stark shifts, intra-dimensional Raman couplings, and cross-dimensional Raman coupling terms, thereby describing multidimensional Raman dynamics beyond a simple superposition of independent single-dimensional models. The framework is used to analyze the principles and operating conditions of two-dimensional atom interferometry. Cross-dimensional Raman coupling and sequential reverse Raman transitions are identified as the main mechanisms that redistribute atoms into non-target momentum states and reduce the contrast of atomic interferometer fringe. Experimentally, Ramsey fringes are observed in a cold-atom fountain interferometer, with a contrast of [MATH] at an interrogation time of [MATH], in good agreement with the theoretical calculation. The conditions required for velocity-sensitive multidimensional atom interferometry are further clarified, including detuning control, velocity-class selection, and suppression of undesired inter-dimensional transitions. This work provides a theoretical and experimental basis for multidimensional Raman atom interferometry.
tldr: Develops a momentum-basis theoretical framework for two-dimensional Raman interactions in atom interferometry.
motivation: To enable multidimensional atom interferometry by coherently controlling atomic wave packets in multiple momentum dimensions.
method: Formulates the atom-laser interaction for 2D Raman beams, derives an effective two-level Hamiltonian on a momentum-state lattice, and analyzes cross-dimensional couplings.
result: Identifies cross-dimensional Raman coupling and sequential reverse Raman transitions as mechanisms that redistribute atoms and reduce fringe contrast; demonstrates Ramsey fringes with contrast matching theory.
conclusion: Provides a theoretical and experimental basis for multidimensional Raman atom interferometry, clarifying conditions for velocity-sensitive operation.

title: Super-Gaussian Approximations For Optimum Far-field Irradiance In Intersatellite Optical Communications: Coherent And Incoherent Beam Shaping
authors: Mario Bad\'as Aldecocea, Yves van Gennip, Pierre Piron, Jasper Bouwmeester, J\'er\^ome Loicq
abstract: ArXiv:2606.15362v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Intersatellite optical communication links are strongly affected by transmitter pointing jitter, which stochastically modulates the received optical power and degrades communication performance. While adjusting the divergence of a conventional Gaussian beams can partially mitigate this effect, the optimum far-field irradiance distribution for maximizing link performance has not been formally derived. In this work, we introduce a variational formalism to determine the optimum far-field irradiance for an intersatellite link affected by pointing jitter. The flat-top beam is found to be the optimum beam shape for minimizing outage probability. In particular, it requires [MATH] of the power needed by a conventional Gaussian beam to achieve the same outage probability. However, the flat-top profile is discontinuous and physically unrealizable. To address this, we analyze a continuous family of super-Gaussian beam shapes that approximate the flat-top as the order increases. In addition, several coherent and incoherent beam shaping techniques are evaluated to assess their ability to reproduce the optimum irradiance distribution. The results show that these techniques can reduce the required transmitted power by up to [MATH] compared with conventional Gaussian beams.
tldr: This paper optimizes far-field irradiance for intersatellite optical communications using super-Gaussian beams to mitigate pointing jitter.
motivation: Intersatellite optical links suffer from pointing jitter; conventional Gaussian beams are suboptimal. The authors seek the optimum beam shape to minimize outage probability.
method: A variational formalism is introduced to derive the optimum far-field irradiance, and super-Gaussian approximations are analyzed. Coherent and incoherent beam shaping techniques are evaluated.
result: The flat-top beam is optimal but unrealizable; super-Gaussian beams can reduce required power by up to 50% compared to Gaussian beams.
conclusion: Super-Gaussian beam shaping significantly improves link performance, but the work is purely classical optical communication with no quantum component.

title: Cvxpy 1.9: Recent Advances In Optimization Modeling Software
authors: William Zhang, Parth Nobel, Aryaman Jeendgar, Riley Murray, Philipp Schiele, Steven Diamond
abstract: ArXiv:2606.14891v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: CVXPY is a Python-embedded domain-specific language for convex optimization that lets users express problems in mathematical notation while the system verifies convexity and reduces valid programs to solver-ready form. This paper reports on the major advances from versions 1.1 through 1.9. These include a unified conic quadratic program (CQP) standard form for canonicalization; a stacked-slices backend that accelerates parameterized programs; first-class support for N-dimensional expressions; explicit sparsity for variables; support for multiple variable attributes; cones/atoms relevant to quantum information theory; and the introduction of disciplined nonlinear programming (DNLP). We outline the design, algorithms, and modeling consequences of these features.
tldr: This paper describes recent updates to CVXPY, a convex optimization modeling language, including new features for conic optimization, parameterized programs, and support for quantum information theory cones.
motivation: CVXPY aims to simplify convex optimization by allowing users to express problems in mathematical notation while automatically verifying convexity and reducing to solver-ready forms.
method: The authors present the design and implementation of new features in CVXPY versions 1.1–1.9, including a unified conic quadratic program standard form, stacked-slices backend, N-dimensional expressions, and disciplined nonlinear programming.
result: The new features improve canonicalization, accelerate parameterized programs, and extend CVXPY's applicability to areas like quantum information theory through new cones and atoms.
conclusion: CVXPY continues to evolve as a powerful tool for convex optimization, with recent advances making it more flexible and efficient for a broader range of applications.

title: Representation Costs In Data Science: Foundations And The Quasi-Banach Spaces Of Deep Neural Networks
authors: Rahul Parhi Greg Ongie
abstract: ArXiv:2606.14954v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a general framework for analyzing representation costs of parametric data-fitting methods through their parameter-space regularizers. From this abstract perspective, we define representation costs for arbitrary parametric models and reveal their induced (native) function spaces. This unifies recent function-space views of data-fitting methods. We also prove that many natural results hold in this abstract setting, including representer theorems for parametric methods on their native spaces. The framework also rigorously connects parametric methods with their equivalent nonparametric descriptions under sufficient overparameterization. Classical methods and their native spaces, such as kernel methods / reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, wavelets / Besov spaces, and shallow neural networks / variation spaces emerge as special cases of our abstract framework. A byproduct of "axiomatizing" the study of representation costs is that we also immediately obtain new results for deep neural networks: For depth-[MATH] feedforward ReLU networks, their induced native spaces are [MATH]-normable quasi-Banach spaces with [MATH]. This reveals that the inductive bias of deep neural networks (as given by the representation cost) cannot be captured by norms for depths [MATH].
tldr: This paper develops a general framework for analyzing representation costs of parametric data-fitting methods, focusing on deep neural networks and their induced function spaces.
motivation: To unify and extend the understanding of representation costs in data science, particularly for deep neural networks, and to reveal their native function spaces.
method: The authors propose an abstract framework that defines representation costs for arbitrary parametric models and connects them to nonparametric descriptions under overparameterization.
result: They show that for deep ReLU networks, the induced native spaces are quasi-Banach spaces that are not normable for depths greater than 2.
conclusion: The framework provides a unified perspective on representation costs and reveals fundamental limitations of norm-based inductive biases in deep learning.

title: A Structure-preserving Adaptive-Rank Approach To The High-Dimensional Wigner-Poisson System
authors: Andrew J. Christlieb, Sining Gong, Jing-Mei Qiu, Nanyi Zheng
abstract: ArXiv:2606.15067v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Wigner-Poisson system is a deterministic phase-space model for quantum kinetic electron dynamics, but high-dimensional simulations are limited by the full 3D3V phase space and the nonlocal Wigner potential. We develop a structure-preserving, sampling-based adaptive-rank solver in hierarchical Tucker format for finite-[MATH] regimes in which Wigner-Poisson solutions exhibit exploitable low-rank structure. The central difficulty is that adaptive compression can destroy the Fourier-Hermitian tensor symmetry required for a real inverse velocity transform and can break discrete global conservation laws. We address these issues with a Fourier-Hermitian-symmetry-aware sampling and mapping procedure and a global moment correction enforcing mass, momentum, and self-consistent total energy. Numerical tests for two-stream instability and strong Landau damping in 2D2V and 3D3V show roundoff-level conservation, preservation of the real-valued inverse transform, and approximately linear scaling with respect to the number of grid points per coordinate over the tested rank range. The results demonstrate that long-time 3D3V Wigner-Poisson simulations can be performed without assembling the full phase-space tensor.
tldr: This paper develops a structure-preserving adaptive-rank solver for the high-dimensional Wigner-Poisson system, focusing on numerical methods for quantum kinetic simulations.
motivation: High-dimensional Wigner-Poisson simulations are computationally expensive due to the full 3D3V phase space and nonlocal potential; the goal is to enable long-time simulations without assembling the full tensor.
method: A sampling-based adaptive-rank solver in hierarchical Tucker format is used, with a Fourier-Hermitian-symmetry-aware sampling procedure and a global moment correction to enforce conservation laws.
result: Numerical tests for two-stream instability and Landau damping in 2D2V and 3D3V show roundoff-level conservation, preservation of real-valued inverse transform, and approximately linear scaling with grid points.
conclusion: The method demonstrates that long-time 3D3V Wigner-Poisson simulations are feasible without full tensor assembly, exploiting low-rank structure.

title: A Uniform-in-time Weakly Convergent Explicit Numerical Method For The Underdamped Langevin Equation With Polynomial Potentials
authors: Diancong Jin
abstract: ArXiv:2606.15175v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The underdamped Langevin equation is a fundamental model in statistical mechanics for sampling Gibbs measures and simulating molecular dynamics, for which numerical methods with uniform-in-time weak convergence are essential for accurately reproducing long-time statistical observables and invariant measures of the underlying dynamics. Currently, such uniform-in-time weak convergence is established for implicit schemes, but remains unknown for explicit ones under polynomially growing potentials. To improve efficiency in long-time simulations, we propose the first explicit numerical method for the underdamped Langevin equation with polynomially growing potentials that is proven to achieve uniform-in-time weak convergence. The explicit numerical method is constructed by introducing a dissipativity on the scalar auxiliary variable (SAV), which we call the DSAV method. The proposed DSAV method enables the approximation of the invariant measure for the underdamped Langevin equation with a precision of [MATH] at a significantly reduced computational cost of [MATH]. In addition, we establish the existence and positivity of the density function of the numerical solution without using the Malliavin calculus. Numerical experiments are performed to verify the theoretical findings and demonstrate the long-time stability of the proposed numerical method.
tldr: Proposes an explicit numerical method for the underdamped Langevin equation with uniform-in-time weak convergence for polynomial potentials.
motivation: Existing explicit methods lack uniform-in-time weak convergence guarantees for polynomially growing potentials, limiting long-time simulation efficiency.
method: Introduces a dissipative scalar auxiliary variable (DSAV) to construct an explicit scheme that preserves the invariant measure.
result: The DSAV method achieves uniform-in-time weak convergence with computational cost O(ε^{-2}) and establishes existence and positivity of the numerical density without Malliavin calculus.
conclusion: The method enables efficient and accurate long-time simulations of underdamped Langevin dynamics for sampling and molecular dynamics.

title: Dual-Network PINNs For Optimal Control: A Reproducible Benchmark On The Mass-Spring-Damper System
authors: Rinaldo Vieira Da Silva Junior Abdeladhim Tahimi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.15271v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work presents a transparent and reproducible benchmark study of a direct dual-network Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) formulation for the optimal control of a mass-spring-damper system. The classical linear-quadratic optimal control problem is solved by two independent classical methods -- Pontryagin's Minimum Principle with single shooting, and direct transcription through trapezoidal collocation -- and recast as a constrained optimization problem solved by two feedforward neural networks: a state network whose boundary conditions are enforced exactly through a composite cubic-and-mask ansatz, and an unconstrained control network. The composite loss combines the physics residual at the collocation points with a trapezoidal approximation of the cost functional, weighted by a single scalar hyperparameter. On the benchmark considered, the PINN reproduces the classical optimal cost to four significant digits, satisfies the terminal state constraints exactly by construction, and produces pointwise state and control errors that fall within the spread of the two classical references. Training is approximately two orders of magnitude slower than classical shooting on this benchmark, which is honestly reported. The contribution is methodological clarity rather than methodological novelty: the formulation and the accompanying Google Colab implementation are intended to lower the barrier to entry for practitioners exploring PINN-based optimal control without prior exposure to adjoint methods or two-point boundary value problems.
tldr: This paper benchmarks a dual-network PINN approach for optimal control of a mass-spring-damper system, focusing on reproducibility and pedagogical clarity rather than novel contributions.
motivation: To provide a transparent and reproducible benchmark for PINN-based optimal control, lowering the barrier for practitioners unfamiliar with adjoint methods.
method: Two feedforward neural networks (state and control) are trained with a composite loss combining physics residual and cost functional approximation, using exact boundary condition enforcement via a cubic-and-mask ansatz.
result: The PINN reproduces classical optimal cost to four significant digits with state/control errors within classical reference spreads, but training is ~100x slower than classical shooting.
conclusion: The formulation is methodologically clear and accessible, but not novel; it serves as a pedagogical tool rather than advancing the state of the art.

title: New Bounds For Covering Codes Under Insertions Or Deletions
authors: Chengfei Xie, Yubo Sun, Gennian Ge
abstract: ArXiv:2606.15379v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Covering codes for insertions and deletions arise naturally in the study of synchronization errors and differ substantially from their classical counterparts in the Hamming metric. In this paper, we study covering codes under insertion and deletion operations. We first show that, in contrast to the equivalence between insertion and deletion correction, insertion covering and deletion covering are not equivalent. We then develop bounds and constructions for insertion and deletion covering codes, with particular emphasis on the large-alphabet regime. For insertion covering codes, we extend a recent combinatorial approach for single insertions and establish a new lower bound for arbitrary fixed insertion radius. For deletion covering codes, we relate the problem to hypergraph covering and prove that the elementary counting lower bound is asymptotically tight when the alphabet size tends to infinity. We further provide a construction of asymptotically optimal non-binary single-deletion covering codes by using differential Varshamov--Tenengolts (VT) codes together with a completion argument. In addition, we study covering codes for burst deletions. We prove that binary differential VT codes are not only capable of correcting two-burst deletions but also have the corresponding covering property, and hence form binary perfect codes for two-burst deletions. Finally, we extend this construction to non-binary alphabets and obtain explicit [MATH]-ary two-burst-deletion covering codes.
tldr: This paper studies covering codes under insertion and deletion operations, establishing bounds and constructions for such codes.
motivation: Covering codes for insertions and deletions are important for synchronization error correction, but their properties differ from classical Hamming metric codes.
method: The authors use combinatorial arguments, hypergraph covering, and differential VT codes to derive lower bounds and explicit constructions.
result: They show insertion and deletion covering are not equivalent, provide tight bounds for large alphabets, and construct optimal non-binary single-deletion covering codes and perfect two-burst-deletion codes.
conclusion: The work advances the theory of covering codes for synchronization errors, with implications for coding theory but not directly for quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: SimAMC: A Fast And Accurate Simulator For Resistive Memory-Based Analog Matrix Computing With Non-Idealities
authors: Junbin Long, Mu Zhou, Saitao Zhang, Yongxiang Li, Zhong Sun
abstract: ArXiv:2606.15322v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Analog matrix computing (AMC) circuits leverage resistive memory arrays to perform matrix operations in a massively parallel manner, providing an efficient approach for accelerating data-intensive tasks. However, hardware non-idealities severely impact computational accuracy, making early-stage simulation vital for reliable performance estimation and design optimization. While open-loop circuits for matrix-vector multiplication are well-studied, closed-loop AMC circuits, which solve matrix equations, are computationally more complex and substantially more sensitive to non-idealities, complicating their simulation. In this work, we present SimAMC, a simulator for resistive memory-based closed-loop AMC circuits. SimAMC is capable of modeling matrix inversion and eigenvector solving in the presence of key non-idealities, including device programming error, data conversion error, thermal noise, operational amplifier input offset, and interconnect resistance. For real-valued matrix computing circuits, an alternating iterative algorithm is designed. SimAMC's effectiveness is validated through comparison with SPICE, showing excellent agreement while also demonstrating a speedup of several orders of magnitude.
tldr: SimAMC is a fast simulator for resistive memory-based analog matrix computing circuits, focusing on closed-loop operations like matrix inversion and eigenvector solving with non-idealities.
motivation: Hardware non-idealities in resistive memory arrays degrade computational accuracy, necessitating early-stage simulation for reliable performance estimation and design optimization.
method: The simulator models closed-loop AMC circuits using an alternating iterative algorithm for real-valued matrices, accounting for device programming error, data conversion error, thermal noise, op-amp offset, and interconnect resistance.
result: SimAMC achieves excellent agreement with SPICE simulations while offering speedups of several orders of magnitude.
conclusion: SimAMC enables efficient and accurate simulation of closed-loop AMC circuits, facilitating design optimization for resistive memory-based analog computing.

title: Quiet Planting For $k$-SAT, Multiple Solutions Of Arbitrary Geometry
authors: Ali Ahmadi, Kiarash Banihashem, Iman Gholami, Mohammad Taghi Hajiaghayi, Jan Olkowski
abstract: ArXiv:2606.15979v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent work on "quiet planting" in combinatorial optimization aims to generate instances with a hidden solution that is hard to recover, typically by making the planted distribution statistically indistinguishable from uniform for specific algorithms, such as statistical queries. A prominent example is planted [MATH]-SAT, where [MATH] clauses can be planted while maintaining indistinguishability from uniform instances, evidenced by prior hardness results which also align with findings in SAT refutation. Despite extensive research and practical use in benchmarking SAT solvers, the challenge of quietly planting multiple solutions while preserving hardness has remained an open problem. This work initiates the study of quiet planting with an arbitrary number of solutions, proposing the first method to construct quiet planting distributions for [MATH]-SAT formulas that accommodate more than one solution. We provide statistical query lower bounds for distinguishing these planted instances from uniform ones, and our method allows for planting solutions with arbitrary geometric relationships, including varying Hamming distances. A key innovation facilitating multiple solutions is the ability to incorporate arbitrary correlations between variable selection in clauses and their negation patterns, departing from prior approaches. We also investigate the worst-case complexity of SAT by showing the difficulty in distinguishing satisfiable instances with numerous solutions from unsatisfiable ones, addressing an open problem of Hsieh, Mohanty, and Xu (CCC'22). Technically, we generalize [MATH]-wise uniformness in clause distributions, proving hardness if marginal negation distributions are [MATH]-wise uniform. We also reveal a connection to binary linear codes, showing a [MATH] code can guide planting up to [MATH] solutions on [MATH] variables.
tldr: This paper introduces a method for quietly planting multiple solutions in k-SAT instances with arbitrary geometry, proving hardness via statistical query lower bounds.
motivation: The goal is to generate hard SAT instances with multiple hidden solutions, which is useful for benchmarking solvers and understanding worst-case complexity.
method: The authors generalize k-wise uniform clause distributions and use binary linear codes to plant multiple solutions while maintaining indistinguishability from uniform instances.
result: They provide statistical query lower bounds for distinguishing planted from uniform instances and show that distinguishing satisfiable instances with many solutions from unsatisfiable ones is hard.
conclusion: This work advances the theory of quiet planting and addresses open problems in SAT refutation and worst-case complexity.

title: Watching Ionization In A New Light
authors: Zhiyuan Wang
Renkai Li
abstract: Nature Photonics, Published online: 05 June 2026;
tldr: MeV electron pulses induce strong modulation in optical transmission of semiconductors, enabling room-temperature detection of ionizing radiation with sub-10-ps timing precision.
motivation: To develop next-generation medical imaging and radiation diagnostics with improved timing resolution.
method: Experimental demonstration using MeV electron pulses and optical transmission measurement in common semiconductors.
result: Observation of surprisingly strong modulation enabling sub-10-ps timing precision at room temperature.
conclusion: The findings could lead to next-generation medical imaging and radiation diagnostics.

title: Is Ball Lightning A Relativistic Soliton?
authors: Sergei Bulanov
abstract: Nature Photonics, Published online: 05 June 2026;
tldr: The paper proposes that ball lightning may be explained by relativistic solitons, supported by laser experiments producing millimeter-scale solitons.
motivation: Ball lightning is a poorly understood atmospheric phenomenon; the paper aims to test whether relativistic solitons can account for its properties.
method: High-power laser experiments are used to generate relativistic solitons in a laboratory setting, and their characteristics are compared to ball lightning observations.
result: Millimeter-scale relativistic solitons are produced, suggesting that such structures could indeed be responsible for ball lightning.
conclusion: Relativistic solitons are a plausible explanation for ball lightning, warranting further investigation.

authors: Furqanul Hassan Naqvi
abstract: Nature Reviews Physics, Published online: 10 June 2026;
tldr: This paper describes a technique for probing lattice dynamics using tandem Fabry–Pérot Brillouin spectroscopy.
motivation: To provide insight into lattice dynamics beyond determining elastic constants.
method: Tandem Fabry–Pérot Brillouin spectroscopy is used to measure phonon spectra.
result: The technique enables detailed characterization of lattice dynamics.
conclusion: Careful Brillouin spectroscopy can reveal more about lattice dynamics than just elastic constants.

authors: Chang Jiang, Fan Yang, Yu Zhao, Jinshan Yang, Peng Yu, Huiying Liu, Yuda Zhang, Zehao Jia, Xiangyu Cao, Li Tian, Jingyi Yan, Zheng Liu, Zhongkai Liu, Xian-Lei Sheng, Cong Xiao, Shengyuan A. Yang, Shaoming Dong, And Faxian Xiu

motivation: To explore nonlinear transport phenomena in topological semimetals and understand the role of Berry curvature in generating nonlinear Hall effects without external magnetic fields.

result: A room-temperature intrinsic nonlinear planar Hall effect is observed, attributed to an orbital mechanism involving the Berry-connection-polarizability dipole.

conclusion: Confirms theoretical predictions of chirality in altermagnets, advancing understanding of magnetic materials.

title: Role Of Anionic Lone-Pair-Like Electrons In Producing Minimum Lattice Thermal Conductivity
authors: Hongwei Ming, Jiahui Wang, Shike Xu, Bushra Jabar, Yunpeng Zheng, Zhong-Zhen Luo, And Zhigang Zou

method: First-principles calculations and experimental measurements on selected materials to analyze phonon dispersion and anharmonicity.
result: Anionic lone-pair-like electrons induce strong lattice anharmonicity, leading to minimum lattice thermal conductivity comparable to amorphous limits.
conclusion: Anionic lone-pair-like electrons provide a new route to design materials with ultralow thermal conductivity for thermoelectrics.

title: Learning The Action For Long-Time-Step Simulations Of Molecular Dynamics
authors: Filippo Bigi, Johannes Spies, And Michele Ceriotti
abstract:
Author(s): Filippo Bigi, Johannes Spies, and Michele Ceriotti

Machine learning can reduce the number of time steps needed to accurately predict the progress of a dynamically evolving system.


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 237301] Published Tue Jun 09, 2026.
tldr: This paper uses machine learning to accelerate molecular dynamics simulations by learning the action for long time steps.
motivation: Molecular dynamics simulations are computationally expensive due to the need for many small time steps; reducing the number of steps while maintaining accuracy would greatly improve efficiency.
method: The authors propose a machine learning approach to learn the action (a quantity related to the trajectory) that allows accurate prediction of system evolution over longer time steps.
result: The method demonstrates that machine learning can effectively reduce the number of time steps needed for accurate molecular dynamics simulations.
conclusion: Learning the action enables longer time steps in molecular dynamics, offering a potential speedup for simulations of complex systems.

title: Lorentz Violation In Emergent Gravity And Its Cosmological Consequences
authors: Raymond Isichei And João Magueijo
abstract:

tldr: This paper interprets general relativity as a degenerate Otto cycle in emergent gravity, leading to Lorentz violation and late-time cosmological acceleration.
motivation: To explore the connection between emergent gravity and thermodynamics, and to derive observable consequences of Lorentz violation.
method: The authors model gravity as an emergent thermodynamic system using an Otto cycle analogy, then introduce work-producing legs to break Lorentz invariance.
result: They find that controlled Lorentz violations can produce late-time cosmic acceleration without dark energy.
conclusion: The emergent gravity framework with thermodynamic cycles offers a novel perspective on cosmology and Lorentz symmetry.

method: The authors fabricate nanoscale tips that generate coherent phonons with tunable frequencies and use them to probe functional materials.
result: They achieve broadband frequency tunability and demonstrate the ability to probe various material properties at the nanoscale.
conclusion: The coherent phonon tips provide a new approach for nanoscale characterization of materials.

title: Alternative Representation Of Multichannel Rydberg Spectra: A Modified $K$-matrix And Lu-Fano Plot Applied To The Manganese Spectroscopy
authors: Justin D. Piel And Chris H. Greene

motivation: Traditional Lu-Fano plots have limitations when there are close-lying channels; the authors aim to improve the graphical representation.
method: They introduce an alternative representation using a modified K-matrix and a new Lu-Fano plot tailored for multichannel Rydberg spectra.
result: The modified approach overcomes some limitations of the traditional Lu-Fano plot, providing clearer visualization of channel interactions.
conclusion: The alternative representation is a useful tool for analyzing complex Rydberg spectra, particularly in atoms like manganese.

title: Th:SBO Single Crystal: A Multifunction Material For Solid-state Nuclear Optical Clocks
authors: Lin Li, Qiaorui Gong, Yuxiang Li, Runzhe Yang, Guoliang Deng, Shanming Li, Peixiong Zhang, Chengchun Zhao, Yin Hang, Longsheng Ma, And Shining Zhu

motivation: To develop a dual-functional platform that combines nonlinear frequency-doubling with a thorium-doped host for nuclear clock applications.
method: Th:SBO single crystals were grown via the Czochralski method, and their structural, electronic, and VUV optical properties were characterized.
result: The crystals exhibit high VUV transmittance and are expected to enable integration of nonlinear optics with a thorium-doped host.
conclusion: Th:SBO is a promising multifunctional material for solid-state nuclear optical clocks.

title: Demonstration Of An Interferometric Technique For Measuring Vacuum Magnetic Birefringence With An Optical Cavity
authors: Aaron D. Spector, Todd Kozlowski, And Laura Roberts

Vacuum magnetic birefringence (VMB) is an effect predicted by quantum electrodynamics in which the vacuum behaves as a nonlinear optical medium and exhibits a birefringence in the presence of a magnetic field. In this work, an interferometric scheme is introduced to measure this effect by sensing th…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 063518] Published Thu Jun 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates an interferometric technique to measure vacuum magnetic birefringence, a QED effect, using an optical cavity.
motivation: Vacuum magnetic birefringence is a predicted QED effect that has not been directly observed; measuring it would test fundamental physics.
method: The authors use an optical cavity to enhance the signal and an interferometric scheme to detect the tiny birefringence induced by a magnetic field.
result: They present a proof-of-principle demonstration and sensitivity analysis, showing the technique can reach the required precision.
conclusion: The interferometric cavity technique is a viable path to measure vacuum magnetic birefringence, potentially confirming QED predictions.

title: Spin Chirality Driven Tunability And Multifunctionality In Two-dimensional Noncollinear Antiferromagnets
authors: Ting Lai, Yongqian Zhu, Jie Zhang, Yuhui Li, Guolin Wan, Xudan Zhang, Jia-Tao Sun, Jinbo Pan, And Shixuan Du

motivation: Noncollinear antiferromagnets are promising for spintronics, but weak spin-orbit coupling magnets have been overlooked. The authors aim to propose a symmetry framework to understand and tune their properties.
method: The authors develop a symmetry-based framework for two-dimensional triangular antiferromagnets with noncollinear spin configurations, likely using first-principles calculations or model Hamiltonians.
result: They demonstrate tunability and multifunctionality driven by spin chirality in these materials.
conclusion: The work provides a pathway for designing high-performance spintronic devices based on weak SOC noncollinear antiferromagnets.

title: Revisiting The Symmetry And Optical Phonons Of Altermagnetic $α$-MnTe
authors: Ece Uykur, Marcos V. Gonçalves-Faria, Sahana Rößler, Victoria A. Ginga, Marcus Schmidt, Stephan Winnerl, Manfred Helm, And Alexander A. Tsirlin

method: Combined infrared and Raman spectroscopies with high-resolution x-ray diffraction, including analysis of mechanical stress effects on Bragg peaks.
result: Mechanical stress broadens Bragg peaks, obscuring additional structural signatures; the study clarifies the phonon spectrum and symmetry properties.
conclusion: The findings resolve ambiguities in the structural and vibrational properties of α-MnTe, contributing to the understanding of altermagnetic materials.

result: The SVD approach provides a systematic way to identify and describe BICs in periodic metasurfaces.
conclusion: The method offers a new tool for designing metasurfaces with tailored resonant properties.

method: Simultaneous measurement of X-ray diffraction peak shift and intensity decay to separate strain and Debye-Waller contributions.
result: Demonstrated that strain and Debye-Waller effects can be disentangled, providing accurate temperature determination on picosecond timescales.
conclusion: The approach enables precise ultrafast thermometry in thin films, useful for studying heat transport and thermal dynamics.

result: The antisymmetric coupling breaks down, leading to nonlinear polarization behavior.
conclusion: The findings challenge the conventional understanding of flexoelectricity and may have implications for electromechanical devices.

method: Density functional theory (DFT) calculations to simulate magnetic phase transitions and magnetocaloric properties.
result: A large inverse magnetocaloric effect is induced by the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction.
conclusion: The findings suggest that 2D ferromagnetic semiconductors with DMI could be promising for magnetic refrigeration applications.

Understanding thermal transport in two-dimensional (2D) materials at cryogenic temperatures is essential for emerging low-temperature nanoelectronics, yet remains largely unexplored because of the lack of a predictive theoretical framework. [Phys. Rev. B 113, 214309] Published Wed Jun 10, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies phonon-mediated thermal transport in 2D MoSe2 at cryogenic temperatures using accelerated ab initio calculations.
motivation: Understanding thermal transport in 2D materials at cryogenic temperatures is important for low-temperature nanoelectronics but lacks a predictive theoretical framework.
method: The authors develop an accelerated, mode-resolved first-principles approach to compute phonon thermal conductivity.
result: They obtain mode-resolved thermal transport properties of monolayer MoSe2 at cryogenic temperatures.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical framework for predicting thermal transport in 2D materials at low temperatures, relevant for nanoelectronics.

tldr: This paper studies the dynamics and pinning of skyrmions in altermagnets using atomistic simulations.
motivation: Skyrmions in altermagnets are a novel type of magnetic texture with potential applications in spintronics, but their dynamics under pinning are not well understood.
method: The authors use an atomistic model to simulate Néel skyrmions in an altermagnet with two sublattices, applying a driving force and measuring velocity and Hall angle.
result: They find that the skyrmion velocity and Hall angle are anisotropic with respect to the drive direction due to the fourfold symmetry of the altermagnet.
conclusion: The anisotropic dynamics and pinning properties could be exploited for skyrmion-based devices, but the work is primarily in condensed matter physics without direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Threshold And Quasistationary Distribution For The Susceptible-infectious-susceptible Model On Networks

[Phys. Rev. E 113, 065410] Published Fri Jun 12, 2026.

motivation: Understanding yielding in dense active matter is important for designing reconfigurable materials and modeling animal collectives, but the paper does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The authors use numerical simulations and theoretical modeling to analyze the mechanical response of dense active granular matter under shear.
result: They identify key similarities and differences between active and passive yielding, and characterize the role of activity on the yielding transition.
conclusion: The work provides insights into the rheology of dense active matter but has no direct relevance to the user's research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Chromatic Percolation In Two-dimensional Multitype Particle Systems With Extended-range Homotypic Repulsion
authors: Tingting Yin, Yan Sui, Xueying Yuan, And Xian Kong

Cells in many tissues repel like neighbors over extended ranges, yet standard jamming models ignore this diversity. motivation: Standard jamming models ignore diversity in cell-cell repulsion ranges; this work aims to understand how homotypic repulsion drives percolation and jamming in multitype assemblies.
method: Develops a chromatic percolation model for two-dimensional multitype particle systems with extended-range homotypic repulsion, analyzed via simulations and theoretical mapping.
result: Finds that extended-range homotypic repulsion can induce percolation of like-type particles, which correlates with mechanical jamming transitions.
conclusion: Chromatic percolation provides a framework to connect percolation and jamming in diverse biological and soft matter systems.

title: Supratransmission In Lattices With Purely Nonlinear Coupling

tldr: This paper studies supratransmission in nonlinear lattices with purely nonlinear coupling, where energy propagation occurs without a linear passband.
motivation: To extend the phenomenon of supratransmission to systems lacking linear spectrum, which is a fundamental nonlinear wave dynamics problem.
method: Analytical and numerical analysis of a lattice model with purely nonlinear coupling, examining energy transmission thresholds and dynamics.
result: Supratransmission is observed even without linear passband, with energy propagation arising solely from nonlinear interactions.
conclusion: The work broadens the understanding of supratransmission to purely nonlinear systems, relevant to nonlinear wave physics.

title: Biased Continuous-time Random Walks With Asymmetric Waiting-time Distributions As A Model Of Anomalous Diffusion In The Presence Of Drift

[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064116] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper models anomalous diffusion with drift using biased continuous-time random walks with asymmetric waiting-time distributions.
motivation: To understand transport in complex media where diffusion is anomalous and influenced by external or internal bias.

result: The model captures anomalous diffusion regimes and the effect of drift on the mean squared displacement and other transport characteristics.

tldr: This paper tests the validity of generalized heterogeneous-elasticity theory for low-frequency excitations in structural glasses, focusing on non-universal scaling of the vibrational density of states.

abstract:
Author(s): Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, and Lorenzo Rigutti

Atomic-scale details, especially those of disorder, are important for material properties, especially in semiconductors, but they are also extremely difficult to measure. Real-space methods can give direct access to this information, but typically, that access is limited. This review reports the application of three real-space techniques for measuring disorder to compound semiconductor materials: scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy.
