method: The authors review scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy, emphasizing combined use for a complete defect picture.
result: The review highlights capabilities and limitations of each technique and cases where they are combined to characterize disorder.
conclusion: Real-space microscopy methods provide direct access to atomic-scale disorder, and combining them yields a more comprehensive understanding.

title: Kovacs-like Memory Effect In Strain Stiffening Collagen Networks
authors: Maitri Mandal And Sayantan Majumdar Abhishek Ghadai
abstract: Materials driven far from equilibrium can encode memories of past deformations through long-lived structural reorganizations. Such memory effects-reflecting parameters such as deformation direction, magnitude, and duration have been widely explored in soft amorphous solids. Here, we report a Kovacs-like memory effect manifested as a non-monotonic stress relaxation in vitro biopolymer networks formed by type-I collagen, an essential component of the mammalian extracellular matrix. Using shear rheology combined with in-situ optical imaging, we find that this memory effect emerges exclusively in the nonlinear strain-stiffening regime, and persists over a much broader range of strain amplitudes than previously reported for other viscoelastic amorphous materials. Furthermore, we uncover a strong correlation between the memory response and the development of negative normal stresses and associated strain fields, highlighting the unique nonequilibrium mechanics underlying memory formation in biopolymer networks.
tldr: This paper reports a Kovacs-like memory effect in strain-stiffening collagen networks, focusing on non-equilibrium mechanics of biopolymer networks.
motivation: To understand memory effects in soft amorphous materials, specifically in biopolymer networks like collagen, which are important for biological tissues.
method: Shear rheology combined with in-situ optical imaging to observe stress relaxation and normal stresses in collagen networks under nonlinear strain-stiffening conditions.
result: A non-monotonic stress relaxation (Kovacs-like memory effect) is observed exclusively in the nonlinear strain-stiffening regime, correlated with negative normal stresses.
conclusion: The memory effect in collagen networks arises from unique non-equilibrium mechanics distinct from other amorphous materials, with potential implications for biological tissue mechanics.

title: Continuous Thermochemical Sources Of AlF Molecules
authors: Pulkit Kukreja, Priyansh Agarwal, Maximilian Doppelbauer, Jionghao Cai, Xiangyue Liu, Eduardo Padilla, Sebastian Kray, Henrik Haak, Russell Thomas, Stefan Truppe, Boris G Sartakov, Gerard Meijer And Sid Wright
abstract: The AlF molecule, currently subject to laser cooling and trapping efforts, has the advantage that it can be efficiently produced in a thermochemical reaction between sublimated aluminum trifluoride and aluminum metal. Here we present a series of experiments with continuous molecular beam sources of AlF, utilizing this reaction. We demonstrate a compact AlF molecular beam oven whose total far-field brightness is molecules per steradian per second at 923 K, just below the melting temperature of aluminum metal. The continuous output from the oven begins to exceed the peak brightness of a jet-cooled, ablation-based supersonic AlF source for the , level, and we obtain an excellent signal-to-noise ratio with the oven in pulsed laser ionization spectroscopy experiments. By delivering flux from the oven into a cryogenic Ne buffer gas cell, we lower the rotational temperature of the beam to around 30 K and reduce its most probable forward velocity from 600 m s to 200 m s . In addition, we demonstrate that AlF can be made in a simple dispenser package, and observe that molecules thermalize to the laboratory temperature after colliding with vacuum chamber walls of the experiment. The resulting transient AlF vapor may enable direct loading of a molecular magneto-optical trap.
tldr: This paper presents experimental development of continuous thermochemical sources for AlF molecules, focusing on molecular beam brightness and cooling for laser cooling and trapping.
motivation: AlF molecules are promising for laser cooling and trapping, but efficient and continuous sources are needed for advanced experiments.
method: The authors built a compact molecular beam oven using a thermochemical reaction between AlF3 and Al, and also tested a dispenser package; they characterized beam brightness, rotational temperature, and velocity using spectroscopy.
result: The oven achieves high brightness (10^11 molecules/sr/s) at 923 K, outperforming ablation-based sources for certain levels; buffer gas cooling reduces rotational temperature to ~30 K and forward velocity to 200 m/s.
conclusion: Continuous thermochemical sources of AlF are viable and can provide high flux for laser cooling and trapping experiments, including potential direct loading of a magneto-optical trap.

title: Crystallography-driven Molecularization Of A Two-dimensional Spin- 3 / ...
authors: Hari Borutta, Tobias Müller, Ronny Thomale, Harald O Jeschke And Yasir Iqbal
abstract: Large-spin two-dimensional magnets are generally expected to develop conventional long-range order once the dominant exchange scale becomes appreciable. The layered spin- maple-leaf compound Na Mn O defies this expectation: despite sizable antiferromagnetic interactions and no evident disorder, it exhibits no magnetic ordering and displays two well-separated thermodynamic crossover scales. We show that this behavior originates from a crystallography-driven molecularization of the magnetic degrees of freedom. The low-symmetry structure partitions the Mn sublattice into inequivalent exchange pathways, generating a pronounced hierarchy that nearly isolates antiferromagnetic hexagons. Magnetic correlations therefore develop in two stages: first within individual hexagons at a scale set by the dominant exchange, and only at much lower temperatures do frustrated inter-hexagon couplings attempt to establish coherence across the lattice. While isolated hexagons reproduce the two-step thermodynamic structure, the experimentally relevant temperature scales emerge only once the hexagons are embedded in the frustrated two-dimensional network. The resulting quantum ground state is magnetically disordered, characterized by strong intra-hexagon correlations and rapidly decaying inter-hexagon correlations. These results identify crystallographic inequivalence as a materials-level mechanism for stabilizing molecularized and quantum-disordered states even in large-spin two-dimensional magnets.
tldr: This paper explains the absence of magnetic order in a large-spin 2D magnet via crystallography-driven molecularization into weakly coupled antiferromagnetic hexagons.
motivation: To understand why the layered spin-3/2 compound NaMn2O3 does not order magnetically despite strong antiferromagnetic interactions and no disorder.
method: The authors perform electronic structure calculations and model the magnetic system using a Heisenberg Hamiltonian with exchange couplings derived from the crystal structure, then analyze the resulting thermodynamic and correlation properties.
result: The low-symmetry crystal structure creates a hierarchy of exchange couplings that effectively isolate antiferromagnetic hexagons, leading to two-stage magnetic correlations and a quantum-disordered ground state.
conclusion: Crystallographic inequivalence can stabilize molecularized and quantum-disordered states in large-spin 2D magnets, offering a materials-level mechanism for frustration without geometric frustration.

title: Bayesian Inversion For Single-shot Spectral-encoded Waveform Reconstruction
authors: Thomas C. Underwood Minsoo Kang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.14936v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spectral encoding enables single-shot measurements of ultrafast transients by mapping temporal information onto the spectrum of a chirped probe. This encoding allows dynamics to be recorded that are beyond the response limits of conventional electronic detectors. However, because the measurements record only spectral intensity, the phase of encoded signals is lost, and dispersion in the detection process introduces waveform distortions that complicate reconstruction and quantitative interpretation of spectra. In single-shot terahertz time-domain spectroscopy (THz-TDS), these distortions manifest as a tradeoff between temporal resolution and the measurement window of signals and can produce spectral null frequencies that limit the recoverable THz bandwidth. To address this challenge, a Bayesian inversion framework is developed to recover the underlying waveform from the squared spectral observable by inferring the THz field, the modulation coefficient, and a low-dimensional empirical parameterization of the probe spectrum jointly, while a Gaussian process prior regularizes the waveform. The framework is validated using single-shot THz-TDS experiments spanning two probe spectral profiles and three chirp conditions with [MATH] ranging from 14.5 to 40 ps[MATH]. Across all cases, the inversion reconstructs both the time-domain waveform and spectral null frequency structure within the credible interval of a delay-line reference measurement. These results establish a pathway to eliminate penalties that are associated with the detection process in spectral encoding methods without adding additional optics or alignment complexity.
tldr: A Bayesian inversion framework for single-shot spectral-encoded waveform reconstruction in terahertz time-domain spectroscopy.
motivation: Spectral encoding enables ultrafast measurements but loses phase information and introduces distortions, limiting temporal resolution and bandwidth.
method: Develops a Bayesian inversion that jointly infers the THz field, modulation coefficient, and probe spectrum using a Gaussian process prior.
result: Validated on experimental data, the method reconstructs waveforms and spectral nulls within credible intervals of reference measurements.
conclusion: Eliminates detection penalties in spectral encoding without additional optics, improving single-shot THz-TDS.

title: Distilling Latent Electrostatics From Foundation Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
authors: Bingqing Cheng Xiaoyu Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.15001v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Foundation machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have enabled atomistic simulations across broad regions of chemical and materials space, but many remain computationally expensive and lack explicit electrostatics, limiting their use for systems governed by long-range interactions and electrical response. Previously, we introduced Latent Ewald Summation (LES), which learns latent atomic charges and long-range electrostatics from density functional theory (DFT) energy and force labels alone. Here, we use LES to extract electrostatics that are latent in foundation models: energies and forces predicted by a teacher model are used to train a lightweight LES-augmented student MLIP, with optional fine-tuning on additional DFT data. The resulting models reduce computational cost while providing access to Born effective charge tensors, and infrared spectra. We benchmark student models distilled from a broad set of foundation MLIPs, including UMA, MACE, Orb, eSEN, GemNet-OC, PET, and EquiformerV2-based models, against experimental infrared spectra for liquid water, concentrated hydrochloric acid, and the anatase TiO2(101)-water interface. Across these systems, electrostatic response can be extracted from most foundation MLIPs. The benchmark further shows that the underlying DFT level and dataset used to train the teacher model play a larger role than architecture in determining electrostatic and spectroscopic accuracy. For the TiO2-water interface, fine-tuning with a modest amount of higher-level DFT data improves structural and infrared predictions. LES-based distillation therefore provides a practical route for converting foundation MLIPs into efficient, electrically responsive models, while also testing the physical fidelity encoded in foundation models.
tldr: This paper distills latent electrostatics from foundation machine learning interatomic potentials using Latent Ewald Summation to create efficient, electrically responsive models for atomistic simulations.
motivation: Foundation MLIPs are computationally expensive and lack explicit electrostatics, limiting their use for systems with long-range interactions and electrical response.
method: The authors use Latent Ewald Summation (LES) to learn latent atomic charges from DFT energy/force labels, then train a lightweight LES-augmented student MLIP using energies and forces predicted by a teacher foundation model, with optional fine-tuning on additional DFT data.
result: The distilled models reduce computational cost while providing Born effective charge tensors and infrared spectra; benchmarked against experimental spectra for water, hydrochloric acid, and TiO2-water interface, showing that the underlying DFT level and dataset matter more than architecture.
conclusion: LES-based distillation offers a practical route to convert foundation MLIPs into efficient, electrically responsive models, while also testing the physical fidelity encoded in foundation models.

title: Finite-Slab Reflectance And Transmittance For Henyey-Greenstein Scattering Via A First-Passage Transfer Operator
authors: R. Cordery C. Zeller
abstract: ArXiv:2606.15025v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We compute the reflectance R and transmittance T of a plane-parallel slab of optical thickness tau for Henyey-Greenstein (HG) scattering with asymmetry parameter g, single-scattering albedo a, and incidence angle theta_0. The method is a Monte-Carlo-free first-passage transfer operator on the depth-direction state (z, mu): exact in formulation, with no physical approximation beyond the transport model, and evaluated by a numerically convergent discretization. A free flight in depth at fixed direction cosine is followed by the azimuthally averaged HG angular redistribution. Confining the operator to (0, tau) with absorbing boundaries yields, in a single evaluation, the order-resolved reflection and transmission laws P_R(n) and P_T(n), from which R and T follow at every albedo through the weighting sum_n P(n) a^n, together with the emergent angular distributions R(mu), T(mu) at no extra cost. Reflectance obeys the factorization R_tau = sum_n P_inf(n) S(n, tau) a^n. Beyond serving as a forward model, the central result is structural: the finite slab recovers the half-space first-return law P_inf(n) order by order as tau -> infinity, placing slab reflectance and the half-space return statistics in one framework. The operator reproduces full three-dimensional Monte Carlo in both channels to <= 1.6 x 10^-3 (absolute) across g in [0, 0.95], tau in [0.5, 16], albedo a in [0.5, 1], and normal-to-oblique incidence, with energy conservation R + T = 1 recovered to < 10^-4 at a = 1.
tldr: This paper computes reflectance and transmittance for Henyey-Greenstein scattering in a slab using a first-passage transfer operator, with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: To provide an exact, Monte-Carlo-free method for computing radiative transfer in scattering media, relevant to atmospheric optics and biomedical imaging.
method: A first-passage transfer operator on the depth-direction state space, combining free flight with azimuthally averaged HG angular redistribution, solved via numerically convergent discretization.
result: Order-resolved reflection and transmission laws are obtained, reproducing Monte Carlo results to high accuracy and recovering half-space statistics in the thick-slab limit.
conclusion: The method offers a structural unification of slab and half-space scattering, but is purely classical and unrelated to the user's research interests.

title: On The Non-Commutative Geometry Of The Electroweak Interaction
authors: Gustavo Amilcar Salda\~na Moncada
abstract: ArXiv:2606.15039v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In differential geometry, the underlying mathematical structure behind the electroweak theory is a trivial principal [MATH]--bundle over [MATH] with the Minkowski metric. The aim of this paper is to show that, using non--commutative geometry, the electroweak theory can be described using a trivial quantum principal [MATH]--bundle over [MATH] with the Minkowski metric.
tldr: This paper uses non-commutative geometry to describe the electroweak interaction as a quantum principal bundle, but it is purely mathematical and unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.
motivation: To reformulate the electroweak theory using non-commutative geometry, providing a new mathematical framework.
method: Constructs a trivial quantum principal U(2)-bundle over Minkowski spacetime using non-commutative differential geometry.
result: Shows that the electroweak interaction can be described within a non-commutative geometric setting.
conclusion: Non-commutative geometry offers an alternative description of the electroweak theory, but no direct implications for quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Toward A Geopolitical Crisis Observatory: Diagnosing Systemic Risk In News Flows Using Complex Systems Science
authors: Didier Sornette
abstract: ArXiv:2606.15081v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Complex-systems science provides media institutions with a rigorous framework to move from reactive reporting to anticipatory diagnosis. Critical events are understood as regime shifts emerging from the interplay between endogenous dynamics and exogenous shocks. Detecting such transitions requires identifying structured precursors, such as changes in correlations, amplification, persistence, and endogeneity, rather than relying on raw signal intensity. Recognizing dragon-king events as regime-generated outliers and incorporating non-normal transient amplification are essential, as is accounting for organizational concealment of risk. A geopolitical crisis observatory would diagnose when systems enter states of heightened susceptibility to cascading disruptions. While state actors are already developing such observatories for strategic purposes, media institutions remain largely reactive. This gap creates a strategic opportunity: leveraging open data and AI embedded within the complex-systems framework developed above, media organizations could transform journalism from reporting to diagnosis, delivering early-warning indicators, scenario-based risk maps, and transparent, data-driven narratives within a new Geopolitical Risk Intelligence Platform.
tldr: This paper proposes using complex systems science to build a geopolitical crisis observatory that diagnoses systemic risk in news flows.
motivation: Media institutions are reactive; the paper argues they could use complex systems tools to anticipate crises.
method: It outlines a framework based on regime shifts, dragon-king events, and non-normal transient amplification, applied to news data.
result: No empirical results; it is a conceptual proposal for a Geopolitical Risk Intelligence Platform.
conclusion: Media organizations should adopt complex-systems diagnostics to move from reporting to anticipatory risk analysis.

title: Atomic Design Transformer: xTB-Validated 3d Molecule Generation From Scaffolds
authors: Takao Kotani
abstract: ArXiv:2606.15220v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present an SE(3)-invariant transformer for 3D-molecule generation, the Atomic Design Transformer (ADT). ADT places atoms one at a time, autoregressively. The SE(3) invariance is achieved by tokenization: each new atom's position is encoded in a local coordinate frame of a previously placed atom. The network is a plain causal transformer. For evaluation, we introduce xTB-Validated Rate (XVR), which checks whether the molecular topology is preserved after xTB GFN2 geometry relaxation. On QM9, ADT is competitive with state-of-the-art baselines. For GEOM-Drugs, we present a quantitative benchmark of scaffold-conditional 3D generation, evaluating seven scaffolds (benzene, pyridine, pyrimidine, pyrazine, furan, thiophene, cyclohexane) on the 30-atom-truncated ground-state GEOM-Drugs dataset. XVR ranges from 11.1% (pyrazine) to 29.7% (benzene), all from a single trained model. The generated molecules are chemically diverse, and generation is fast by virtue of the plain causal-transformer backbone. Application to the 50-atom-truncated GEOM-Drugs dataset yields lower XVR while the per-bond and per-angle quality is retained. These results position ADT as a practical proposer for in silico molecular design.
tldr: An SE(3)-invariant transformer for 3D molecule generation from scaffolds, validated with xTB geometry relaxation.
motivation: To generate chemically valid 3D molecules conditioned on scaffolds for in silico molecular design.
method: Uses a causal transformer with tokenized atom positions in local coordinate frames to achieve SE(3) invariance, and introduces xTB-Validated Rate (XVR) for evaluation.
result: Competitive on QM9; on GEOM-Drugs, XVR ranges from 11.1% to 29.7% across scaffolds from a single model.
conclusion: ADT is a practical and fast proposer for scaffold-conditional 3D molecule generation.

title: The Standard Model Gauge Group From The Exceptional Jordan Algebra
authors: Paul Schwahn John C. Baez
abstract: ArXiv:2606.15235v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct the Standard Model gauge group using the exceptional Jordan algebra [MATH] and its automorphism group [MATH]. The group [MATH] acts on pairs of Jordan subalgebras [MATH] with [MATH] and [MATH], and for any such pair the stabilizer of [MATH] intersected with the identity component of the stabilizer of [MATH] is isomorphic to the Standard Model gauge group. Since [MATH] is the Jordan algebra of observables of a qubit and [MATH] is the Jordan algebra of observables of a qutrit, we could say [MATH] is the Jordan algebra of observables of an 'octonionic qutrit'. In this language our result says roughly that the Standard Model gauge group is the group of symmetries of an octonionic qutrit that restrict to act as unitary operators on an ordinary qutrit and, within that, a qubit.
tldr: This paper constructs the Standard Model gauge group from the exceptional Jordan algebra and its automorphism group, relating it to an octonionic qutrit.
motivation: To derive the Standard Model gauge group from a mathematical structure (exceptional Jordan algebra) that may underlie quantum theory.
method: The authors study the action of the automorphism group of the exceptional Jordan algebra on pairs of subalgebras, and compute the stabilizer subgroup.
result: The stabilizer of a qutrit subalgebra intersected with the identity component of the stabilizer of a qubit subalgebra is isomorphic to the Standard Model gauge group.
conclusion: The Standard Model gauge group can be understood as the symmetry group of an octonionic qutrit that restricts to unitary operations on an ordinary qutrit and qubit.

title: The Regional Boundary Reconstruction Problem Of The Initial State For Fractional Semilinear Systems
authors: Khalid Zguaid, Fatima Zahrae El Alaoui, Delfim F. M. Torres
abstract: ArXiv:2606.14705v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Observability is a fundamental concept in control theory. Its primary purpose is to look into whether it is possible to reconstruct the system's initial state using only the information from its outputs. This paper focuses on the regional reconstruction problem of the initial state for a semilinear time-fractional system, which refers to the possibility of recovering the value of the initial state on a desired boundary sub-region instead of the whole evolution domain or its boundary. To achieve this objective, we use the analytical method, where we suppose that the system's dynamic generates an analytic semigroup. First, by establishing an internal sub-region, we establish a connection between the concepts of regional observability and regional boundary observability; we will later explain how to define the internal sub-region. Then, by imposing suitable assumptions on the analytic semigroup and the system's non-linearity, we give the main theorems of this research from which we deduce a sequence that converges to the unknown initial state on the desired boundary sub-region. Moreover, we present an algorithm that produces some numerical simulations which align closely with our theoretical findings.
tldr: This paper studies regional boundary observability and reconstruction of initial states for fractional semilinear systems using analytic semigroups.
motivation: To recover the initial state on a boundary sub-region of a fractional semilinear system, which is a problem in control theory.
method: Uses analytical methods assuming the system generates an analytic semigroup, establishes a connection between regional observability and regional boundary observability via an internal sub-region, and derives a convergent sequence for the unknown initial state.
result: Provides main theorems and an algorithm with numerical simulations that validate the theoretical findings.
conclusion: The proposed method successfully reconstructs the initial state on a desired boundary sub-region for fractional semilinear systems.

title: On Fuzzy Partial Differential Equations For A-Linearly Interactive Fuzzy Complex Processes: Sobolev Spaces And Fourier Analysis
authors: Silvio Antonio Bueno Salgado, Estev\~ao Esmi, Francielle Santo Pedro Sim\~oes, La\'ecio Carvalho de Barros
abstract: ArXiv:2606.14774v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This article develops a mathematical framework to handle fuzzy partial differential equations (PDEs) using Sobolev spaces defined over A-linearly interactive complex fuzzy processes. We introduce the notion of weak derivative in the fuzzy sense to define fuzzy Sobolev spaces that preserve key analytical properties. Furthermore, we introduce a fuzzy Fourier transform adapted to this context and explore its main properties. Applications to fuzzy versions of the heat and Schr\"odinger equations are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness and generality of the proposed framework. This approach not only extends classical tools to the fuzzy setting, but also provides new insights into the treatment of uncertainty in dynamic systems.
tldr: This paper develops fuzzy Sobolev spaces and Fourier analysis for fuzzy partial differential equations, applied to fuzzy heat and Schrödinger equations.
motivation: To extend classical PDE tools to handle uncertainty in dynamic systems using fuzzy set theory.
method: Introduces weak derivatives in the fuzzy sense to define fuzzy Sobolev spaces and a fuzzy Fourier transform for A-linearly interactive complex fuzzy processes.
result: Establishes a mathematical framework that preserves key analytical properties and demonstrates applicability to fuzzy versions of the heat and Schrödinger equations.
conclusion: The framework effectively generalizes classical PDE methods to fuzzy settings, offering new insights for modeling uncertainty.

title: Mapping Mathematical Hardness: Machine-Assisted Conjecture Discovery And The Quantification Of Non-Triviality
authors: Madhuparna Das
abstract: ArXiv:2606.14804v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine-assisted mathematical discovery has been a long-standing challenge in machine learning and artificial intelligence. In recent years, we have seen tremendous progress with generative AI, yet its contribution to automated discovery in advanced mathematical research has been limited. One of the most difficult benchmarks in this context is the Birch test, which asks whether a machine can discover truly novel and non-trivial mathematical structures without human intervention. In this work, we particularly focus on the branch of automated conjecture discovery. We use HypothesiX, an automated conjecture mining agent and analyse its generated conjectures related to the distribution of twin primes to verify the conditions of the Birch test. Furthermore, note that automated discovery is now operating at scale, but verifying its non-triviality still depends on human evaluation. We propose a benchmark to quantify the non-triviality of machine-generated conjectures using the Mahalanobis distance within an embedding cluster of selected known mathematical conjectures. We also note that this quantified benchmark can be used as an error indication signal to localise the incorrectness of a new mathematical statement, which autoformalisers fail to verify due to their limitations in proof discovery capability.
tldr: This paper uses a machine learning agent to generate conjectures about twin primes and proposes a metric to quantify non-triviality of mathematical statements.
motivation: To automate mathematical discovery and verify the Birch test for machine-generated conjectures, and to reduce reliance on human evaluation of non-triviality.
method: Uses HypothesiX, an automated conjecture mining agent, to generate conjectures about twin prime distribution, and proposes a Mahalanobis distance-based benchmark to quantify non-triviality within an embedding cluster of known conjectures.
result: The generated conjectures are analyzed against the Birch test conditions, and a quantitative non-triviality measure is introduced that can also serve as an error signal for autoformalizers.
conclusion: The proposed benchmark can help automate the verification of machine-generated mathematical conjectures and localize incorrect statements.

title: A Transformer-Based Mixture-of-Experts Framework For False Data Injection Attack Detection And Localization
authors: Mohammad Rasoul Narimani Ruslan Abdulin
abstract: ArXiv:2606.15005v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: False data injection attacks (FDIAs) threaten smart-grid operation by manipulating measurement data and misleading power system state estimation. Although recent data-driven methods have shown promising performance, many existing approaches rely on a single graph-filtering mechanism and therefore struggle to adapt to diverse cyberattack patterns. This paper proposes a topology-aware encoder-only transformer mixture-of-experts framework for joint FDIA detection and localization. The proposed model integrates Laplacian positional encoding and diffusion-biased self-attention to capture global spatial dependencies, while a densely routed mixture-of-experts module composed of Chebyshev and autoregressive moving-average graph convolutional experts adaptively applies complementary graph filters based on the current grid state. The framework is evaluated on the IEEE 118- and 300-bus systems using the New York Independent System Operator load profile. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves up to 93.91% detection F1 score and 84.97% localization F1 score, outperforming existing benchmark methods while maintaining low false-alarm rates.
tldr: A transformer-based mixture-of-experts framework for detecting and localizing false data injection attacks in smart grids.
motivation: Existing data-driven methods for FDIA detection struggle to adapt to diverse cyberattack patterns due to reliance on a single graph-filtering mechanism.
method: Proposes a topology-aware encoder-only transformer with Laplacian positional encoding, diffusion-biased self-attention, and a densely routed mixture-of-experts module combining Chebyshev and autoregressive moving-average graph convolutional experts.
result: Achieves up to 93.91% detection F1 score and 84.97% localization F1 score on IEEE 118- and 300-bus systems, outperforming benchmark methods.
conclusion: The framework effectively captures global spatial dependencies and adaptively applies complementary graph filters for improved FDIA detection and localization.

title: A Hankel Determinant Zero-order Principle For Source Counting In An Inverse Heat Point-source Problem
authors: Zhiliang Deng, Ailin Qian, Xiaomei Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.15065v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies the identification of an unknown number of stationary point sources in a two-dimensional heat equation from boundary flux measurements. Unlike many reconstruction approaches that assume the number of sources to be known in advance, we develop a determinant-based counting method that extracts this number directly from the measured data. In the unit disk, the Laplace-transformed and normalized boundary flux admits a Fourier moment representation whose low-frequency limit has a finite exponential-sum structure. This structure leads to a family of Hankel matrices and associated determinant characteristics. We prove that, under a generic determinant lifting condition, the vanishing order of the Hankel determinant at the zero Laplace frequency changes exactly when the Hankel order exceeds the true number of sources. Consequently, the source number is characterized by the first nonzero contour count of the determinant characteristic through the argument principle. We further establish a Rouch\'e-type stability result showing that the determinant zero count is preserved under sufficiently small perturbations induced by measurement noise, boundary discretization, and time truncation. After the source number is identified, the source locations and strengths are recovered from the low-frequency moment sequence by an annihilating-polynomial and Vandermonde reconstruction procedure. Numerical experiments confirm the predicted count pattern, demonstrate robustness with respect to contour selection, illustrate the role of the Rouch\'e margin under noise and near-degenerate configurations, and validate the subsequent recovery of source locations and strengths.
tldr: This paper develops a Hankel determinant method to count the number of point heat sources from boundary flux measurements in an inverse heat conduction problem.
motivation: Many inverse heat source problems assume the number of sources is known, but this work aims to determine the number directly from data.
method: The Laplace-transformed boundary flux is represented as a Fourier moment sequence, leading to Hankel matrices whose determinant's zero-order at zero frequency reveals the source count via the argument principle.
result: The source number is identified by the first nonzero contour count of the determinant characteristic, and a Rouché-type stability result ensures robustness under noise and discretization.
conclusion: The method successfully counts sources and subsequently recovers their locations and strengths, validated by numerical experiments.

title: Two-Timescale Design For Downlink Multiuser Transmission With Dynamic Metasurface Antennas
authors: Hao Xu, Angel Lozano, Hongwen Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.15183v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dynamic metasurface antennas (DMAs) promise to relieve massive multiple-input multiple-output architectures from their high energy consumption and hardware costs. This paper proposes a two-timescale design for downlink multiuser transmission via DMAs, a design that balances pilot overhead, complexity, and spectral efficiency. At the onset of each frame, the DMA coefficients are configured based only on statistical channel-state information (CSI), a process for which the paper introduces an optimization framework that is shown to outperform the widely used stochastic successive convex approximation method. Then, within each frame, the digital precoder is updated at each slot, based on the optimized DMA coefficients and the effective lower-dimensional instantaneous CSI. The weighted minimum mean-squared error method is applied for this short-term optimization and, for the special case of single-user transmission, a closed-form solution for the digital precoder is provided. Performance evaluations demonstrate that the proposed two-timescale design can be an attractive ingredient for future wireless networks.
tldr: This paper proposes a two-timescale design for downlink multiuser transmission using dynamic metasurface antennas to reduce pilot overhead and complexity.
motivation: Massive MIMO systems suffer from high energy consumption and hardware costs; DMAs offer a low-cost alternative but require efficient resource allocation.
method: The DMA coefficients are configured based on statistical CSI at the frame level, while the digital precoder is updated per slot using instantaneous CSI and weighted MMSE.
result: The proposed optimization framework outperforms stochastic successive convex approximation, and for single-user case a closed-form precoder is derived.
conclusion: The two-timescale design balances pilot overhead, complexity, and spectral efficiency, making DMAs attractive for future wireless networks.

title: Intertwining Of $*$-regular $q$-isometric Dilations
authors: Nitin Tomar
abstract: ArXiv:2606.15326v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A tuple [MATH] of contractions on a Hilbert space [MATH] is said to be [MATH]-commuting with [MATH] if there exists a family of scalars [MATH]. In this article, we characterize [MATH]-commuting pairs of contractions with [MATH] that admit a minimal [MATH]-regular [MATH]-isometric dilation. We present sufficient conditions for the commutant lifting theorem for such pairs. Moreover, sufficient conditions are obtained for a [MATH]-commuting triple of contractions with [MATH] to admit a [MATH]-isometric dilation.
tldr: This paper studies operator-theoretic properties of contractions admitting q-isometric dilations, with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.
motivation: The work is motivated by pure mathematics, specifically dilation theory and commutant lifting for non-commuting operator tuples.
method: The authors characterize q-commuting contractions that admit minimal *-regular q-isometric dilations using operator-theoretic techniques.
result: Sufficient conditions are given for the existence of such dilations and for a commutant lifting theorem for pairs and triples of contractions.
conclusion: The results extend known dilation theory to a more general class of operator tuples, but have no apparent application to the user's research areas.

title: An RRAM-based Hardware Implementation Of A Radial Basis Function Neuron For Edge Classifiers
authors: Georgios Papandroulidakis, Shady Agwa, Themis Prodromakis
abstract: ArXiv:2606.14739v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The deployment of modern machine learning (ML) solutions on resource-constrained edge devices highlights implementation challenges. This is especially true for extreme edge applications that include safety-critical components, such as autonomous navigation tasks. This paper demonstrates an artificial neural network (ANN) design leveraging Metal-Oxide Resistive RAM (RRAM) -based Analogue Content Addressable Memory (ACAM) as an efficient hardware substrate for performing metric-based classification and online adaptation on the edge. The proposed design is based on a custom Template piXeL (TXL) cell used for building the ACAM module, where each TXL cell acts as a configurable receptive field neuron. These cells employ a Radial Basis activation function to calculate the distance of an input from the programmed receptive field. The TXL can be organised into dense arrays for calculating the distance of a high-dimensional input against all stored prototypes, effectively performing fast and energy efficient similarity search. This hardware engine enables on-the-fly learning, where the receptive field parameters can be tuned to track domain shift. Through simulation of the proposed TXL-RBF classifier we can achieve 89.1\% accuracy on the MNIST dataset while consuming 185fJ per cell per operation when operating at 100MHz.
tldr: This paper presents an RRAM-based hardware implementation of a radial basis function neuron for edge machine learning classifiers.
motivation: Deploying ML on resource-constrained edge devices is challenging, especially for safety-critical applications like autonomous navigation.
method: The design uses Metal-Oxide Resistive RAM (RRAM) based Analogue Content Addressable Memory (ACAM) with a custom Template piXeL (TXL) cell that implements a radial basis activation function for metric-based classification.
result: The TXL-RBF classifier achieves 89.1% accuracy on MNIST while consuming 185 fJ per cell per operation at 100 MHz.
conclusion: The proposed hardware accelerator enables fast, energy-efficient similarity search and online learning on the edge.

title: Continual Backdoor Training In IoT/CPS
authors: Kuniyilh S Oxana Salish
abstract: ArXiv:2606.14987v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Internet of Things (IoT) and Cyber-physical systems (CPS) increasingly rely on continual learning (CL) to adapt to evolving environments, device heterogeneity, and concept drift, thereby improving overall utility. While continual adaptation is essential for long-lived IoT deployments where data patterns evolve, it also introduces new security vulnerabilities. In particular, backdoor attacks can exploit incremental updates, replay buffers, and representation reuse to implant persistent malicious behaviors that remain dormant during normal operation but activate upon specific triggers. In this paper, we present a backdoor attack in continual learning used in IoT/CPS systems. To this end, we formalize an IoT/CPS-specific threat model, analyze why continual learning amplifies backdoor persistence in IoT pipelines, and evaluate our technique under varying conditions. Our analysis highlights critical open challenges in securing lifelong learning in IoT/CPS and industrial IoT (IIoT) environments, as well as the need for heightened security controls.
tldr: This paper presents a backdoor attack in continual learning for IoT/CPS systems, focusing on security vulnerabilities rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: IoT/CPS systems rely on continual learning to adapt, but this introduces security vulnerabilities such as backdoor attacks that can persist through incremental updates.
method: The authors formalize an IoT/CPS-specific threat model and analyze why continual learning amplifies backdoor persistence, evaluating their attack under varying conditions.
result: The analysis highlights critical open challenges in securing lifelong learning in IoT/CPS and industrial IoT environments.
conclusion: There is a need for heightened security controls to protect against backdoor attacks in continual learning systems.

title: GPU-Accelerated Search And Certification Of Bounded Indistinguishability In Finite Kripke Semantics
authors: Baris Basaran Faruk Alpay
abstract: ArXiv:2606.15437v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study finite Kripke semantics as an explicit search and certification problem for modal formulas. Sets of worlds are encoded as integer bitmasks, so Boolean connectives, [MATH], and [MATH] reduce to word-level containment and intersection tests. This gives a deterministic evaluator with an independent certificate checker, then scales it through a fused CUDA kernel for exhaustive small-frame scans. Over [MATH], a corpus of 5,624 formulas is evaluated on all frames through five worlds, performing [MATH] formula evaluations in 45 minutes on one H100. All 20,990 emitted countermodel certificates verify. In this bounded corpus, every [MATH]-refutable formula has a countermodel on at most two worlds, far below the standard filtration bound [MATH]. We then turn pairwise formula equivalence into a minimal-countermodel problem for biconditionals and synthesize semantic mirages: formulas that agree on every model up to a finite size and split only later. In particular, [MATH] and [MATH] agree on all frames of at most five worlds but are separated by a checked six-world path. Finally, we build a density-aggregated semantic atlas for representation-guided candidate retrieval and compare raw features, PCA, UMAP, spectral layouts, and random layouts under a common million-pair verifier budget. The result is a reproducible bridge between modal finite-model theory, GPU enumeration, certificate checking, and graphics-supported semantic exploration.
tldr: This paper uses GPU acceleration to exhaustively search finite Kripke frames for modal logic formulas, certifying countermodels and studying semantic indistinguishability.
motivation: To bridge modal finite-model theory with high-performance computing for exhaustive verification and exploration of modal formulas.
method: Encodes worlds as bitmasks, reduces modal operators to word-level operations, and implements a fused CUDA kernel for parallel evaluation over all small frames.
result: Evaluated 5,624 formulas on all frames up to 5 worlds in 45 minutes on one H100 GPU; found that all refutable formulas have countermodels on at most 2 worlds, and discovered semantic mirages that agree up to 5 worlds but differ at 6.
conclusion: GPU enumeration enables exhaustive certification and discovery of semantic phenomena in modal logic, with potential for broader applications in logic and verification.

title: Multi-tier Differential Private Query Release
authors: Shaowei Wang, Jinn Li, Yun Peng, Puning Zhao, Wenqi Ren, Changyu Dong, Jin Li, Jian Weng
abstract: ArXiv:2606.15543v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Answering statistical queries over sensitive data under differential privacy (DP) is a common task in many settings, including databases, mobile computing, and data markets. In these scenarios, multiple analysts may issue the same query, while receiving answers generated under different privacy budgets due to differences in trust levels or willingness to pay. Existing approaches for such multi-tier DP queries either incur excessive cumulative privacy loss or suffer from suboptimal utility. In this paper, we propose a framework for multi-tier DP query release that simultaneously bound the cumulative privacy loss by the maximum privacy budget among all queries and achieve optimal utility comparable to that of single-tier mechanisms. Our framework applies to different classes of DP mechanisms. For noise-adding mechanisms (e.g., count queries with the two-sided Geometric mechanism in the curator model), we develop a general solution based on the characteristic functions of noise distributions. For other mechanisms (e.g., count queries under the local DP model with the Subset mechanism), we design mechanism-specific primitives for budget transformation and introduce a template-based strategy that attains optimal utility across different privacy regimes. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework.
tldr: This paper proposes a framework for multi-tier differential privacy query release that bounds cumulative privacy loss and achieves optimal utility.
motivation: Multiple analysts may issue the same query under different privacy budgets, leading to excessive cumulative privacy loss or suboptimal utility in existing approaches.
method: The framework uses characteristic functions of noise distributions for noise-adding mechanisms and mechanism-specific primitives for other mechanisms like the Subset mechanism.
result: The framework simultaneously bounds cumulative privacy loss by the maximum privacy budget and achieves optimal utility comparable to single-tier mechanisms.
conclusion: The proposed framework effectively handles multi-tier DP queries with improved privacy-utility trade-offs.

title: Twin-in-the-Loop Optimization And Fundamental Limits Of Position--Velocity Estimation In Cell-Free Isac Systems
authors: Changhao He, Xiaojuan Zhang, Geoffrey Ye Li
abstract: ArXiv:2606.15688v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Digital twin (DT) networks require tight integration with wireless sensing, yet the fundamental limits of such coupling in cell-free integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) systems remain largely unexplored, particularly in the presence of fluid intelligent metasurfaces (FIM). This paper establishes a joint position-velocity Cramer-Rao bound (CRB) framework, operationalized through a twin-in-the-loop architecture. By leveraging a scatter-matrix decomposition of the velocity Fisher information, we show that single-base-station systems are inherently rank-deficient for two-dimensional velocity estimation, whereas cell-free deployments with multiple access-point pairs achieve full observability. The resulting CRB reveals a spatio-temporal decoupling: FIM shape optimization significantly improves position accuracy but does not affect the velocity CRB under isotropic waveforms while Doppler coupling asymmetrically enhances position estimation accuracy. Building on this analysis, we develop a closed-loop DT framework, deriving the critical mismatch angle in closed form and showing that angular diversity in cell-free systems mitigates DT prediction errors. We further characterize the optimal synchronization period and propose a confidence-aware scheduling strategy that reduces the DT update rate. Numerical results demonstrate substantial performance gains over single-base-station systems, with improvements attributed to angular diversity, Doppler-position coupling, and FIM adaptation.
tldr: This paper studies joint position-velocity estimation in cell-free ISAC systems using digital twins and fluid intelligent metasurfaces, deriving Cramér-Rao bounds and scheduling strategies.
motivation: Digital twin networks require tight integration with wireless sensing, but fundamental limits of such coupling in cell-free ISAC systems with FIM are unexplored.
method: Establishes a joint position-velocity CRB framework via scatter-matrix decomposition of velocity Fisher information, and develops a closed-loop digital twin architecture with confidence-aware scheduling.
result: Single-BS systems are rank-deficient for 2D velocity estimation; cell-free deployments achieve full observability. FIM shape optimization improves position accuracy but not velocity CRB under isotropic waveforms.
conclusion: Angular diversity, Doppler-position coupling, and FIM adaptation in cell-free ISAC systems yield substantial performance gains over single-BS systems.

title: Odds Law: The Decomposition Algebra On How Intelligence Organizes Itself To Solve Difficult Problems Reliably
authors: Hidayet Aksu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.15712v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We ask a structural question: given unreliable elementary problem-solvers, what organizations of them solve hard problems reliably, and what are the limits? We develop a [MATH]: elementary solvers are morphisms in a stochastic category, and four combinators (sequential composition, parallel ensembling, verification gating, and recursive reduction) generate the space of compound solvers. We equip this algebra with two homomorphisms, a [MATH] valuation into the ordered monoid [MATH] and a [MATH] valuation into a commutative semiring, and we derive the composition laws that govern how reliability flows through structure. Our central results are (i) a [MATH] (the result that names this report), showing that a verification gate multiplies the odds of correctness by the verifier's likelihood ratio [MATH], so that [MATH] conditionally independent gates yield geometric amplification; (ii) a [MATH], giving target reliability [MATH] at [MATH] verification depth whenever [MATH]; and (iii) a [MATH]: above the critical parameters reliability can be driven arbitrarily close to one at logarithmic cost, while at or below them no amplification is possible. We then show that [MATH] is the least fixed point of a monotone improvement operator on the complete lattice of strategies, and that this fixed point equalizes marginal log-odds gain per unit cost. Finally, we prove matching limits: an information ceiling bounds per-gate amplification by a divergence quantity; shared error causes create a strictly positive voting floor, so diversity is [MATH] for unbounded amplification. Reliability, in short, is neither free nor magical: it is bought with independent information, arranged by composition, and bounded by the verifier.
tldr: The paper develops an algebraic framework for composing unreliable problem-solvers into reliable systems, deriving laws for reliability amplification through verification gates.
motivation: To understand how intelligence can be organized to solve hard problems reliably using unreliable components.
method: Introduces a stochastic category with four combinators and two homomorphisms, deriving composition laws for reliability.
result: Proves the Odds Law, a threshold theorem, and a cost theorem showing geometric amplification of odds with independent verification gates.
conclusion: Reliability is bought with independent information, arranged by composition, and bounded by the verifier's quality.

title: New Ideas On A New Old Type Of Cipher:The Mixed-Radix One-Time Pad
authors: Fabio F. G. Buono
abstract: ArXiv:2606.16040v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In a short 2012 preprint, an unconventional cipher was introduced, now in this note we take that representational core, formalize it, and use it as the basis for a clean generalization of the one-time pad to non-uniform bases, which we call the Mixed-Radix One-Time Pad (MR-OTP). And we prove that the MR-OTP achieves Shannon perfect secrecy, show that the classical binary OTP is exactly the all-bases-equal-2 special case, and that fixed-base variants recover OTPs over arbitrary alphabets. We then examine whether secret bases can lower the key entropy required for perfect secrecy (they cannot). We close with a usable session protocol based on key rolling that preserves perfect secrecy, and with an honest account of the open problems.
tldr: The paper generalizes the one-time pad to non-uniform bases (mixed-radix) and proves it achieves Shannon perfect secrecy, but it is a classical cryptographic result with no quantum information or thermodynamics content.
motivation: To formalize and extend an unconventional cipher from a 2012 preprint into a clean generalization of the one-time pad for non-uniform alphabets.
method: The authors define the Mixed-Radix One-Time Pad (MR-OTP) using mixed-radix representation and prove its perfect secrecy via Shannon's definition, showing the binary OTP is a special case.
result: The MR-OTP achieves Shannon perfect secrecy, and secret bases do not reduce the key entropy required for perfect secrecy.
conclusion: The MR-OTP is a valid classical cipher with perfect secrecy, but it does not involve quantum mechanics or thermodynamics.

However, the underlying origin of their elasticity—whether it arises from p…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 236102] Published Thu Jun 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper quantifies lattice strains in elastically deformed covalent crystals using experimental and computational methods.
motivation: Understanding the origin of ultralarge elastic strains in covalent semiconductors is important for strain-engineered electronic and optoelectronic devices.
method: The authors combine experimental measurements with theoretical modeling to analyze lattice strains in deformed covalent crystals.
result: They identify the underlying mechanisms of elasticity and quantify strain distributions.
conclusion: The findings provide insights into the elastic behavior of covalent crystals at micro and nanoscales.

title: Mass Probe Of Tetrahedral Symmetry In Atomic Nuclei
authors: F. F. Xu (许方方) And P. W. Zhao
abstract:
Author(s): F. F. Xu (许方方) and P. W. Zhao (赵鹏巍)

Tetrahedral symmetry has long been predicted as an exotic shape degree of freedom in atomic nuclei, yet clear experimental manifestations remain elusive. We show that the triple binding energy difference [MATH] can isolate a structural effect of tetrahedral symmetry in [MATH].…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 232503] Published Wed Jun 10, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a triple binding energy difference as a probe for tetrahedral symmetry in atomic nuclei.
motivation: Tetrahedral symmetry in atomic nuclei has been predicted but lacks clear experimental evidence.
method: The authors use theoretical calculations of binding energies to isolate a structural effect of tetrahedral symmetry.
result: They show that a specific triple binding energy difference can serve as a signature of tetrahedral symmetry.
conclusion: This provides a new experimental observable to search for tetrahedral symmetry in nuclei.

title: Electrical Switching Of Strain Gradients And 90° Domain Walls Via Hidden Polar-Acoustic Coupling In ${\mathrm{PbTiO}}_{3}$
authors: Yajun Zhang, Konstantin Shapovalov, Xu He, Chang Liu, Huadong Yong, Xingyi Zhang, Jie Wang, Kun Zhou, And Philippe Ghosez

Although strain gradients hold great promise for tailoring emergent functionalities, their flexible global control remains a fundamental challenge. Here, we address this concern in [MATH] under biaxial tensile strain by uncovering the spontaneous appearance of strain gradients and 90…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 236101] Published Tue Jun 09, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies strain gradients and domain wall switching in PbTiO3 under biaxial tensile strain via first-principles calculations.
motivation: To achieve flexible global control of strain gradients in ferroelectrics, which is challenging but promising for emergent functionalities.
method: First-principles calculations based on density functional theory to investigate the spontaneous appearance of strain gradients and 90° domain walls in PbTiO3 under biaxial tensile strain.
result: Discovery of hidden polar-acoustic coupling that enables electrical switching of strain gradients and 90° domain walls.
conclusion: The findings provide a mechanism for controlling strain gradients electrically, which may enable new functionalities in ferroelectric materials.

title: Effects Of Screening And Pressure Ionization On The Electron Broadening Of Spectral Lines In Dense Plasmas
authors: J. P. Kinney, S. B. Hansen, T. A. Gomez, And S. D. Baalrud
abstract:

Collisions between electrons and radiating atoms broaden spectral absorption and emission lines in dense plasmas. [Phys. Rev. A 113, 062804] Published Thu Jun 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies electron broadening of spectral lines in dense plasmas, focusing on screening and pressure ionization effects.
motivation: Understanding spectral line shapes in dense plasmas is important for plasma diagnostics, but the paper does not connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
method: The authors model collisions between electrons and radiating atoms, incorporating screening and pressure ionization to compute line broadening.
result: They quantify how dense plasma effects alter the wave functions and collision rates, affecting spectral line profiles.
conclusion: The work provides improved models for spectral line broadening in dense plasmas, but has no relevance to the user's research interests.

title: Unified Treatment Of Direct And Resonant Scattering In Low-energy $\text{electron}\text{−}{\mathrm{H}}_{2}$ Vibrational Excitation: Boomerang Oscillations And The $υ=0→1$ Excitation
authors: Liam H. Scarlett, Nathan A. Garland, Gregory J. Boyle, Dale L. Muccignat, Ronald D. White, Mark C. Zammit, Ilkhom B. Abdurakhmanov, Maciej Cytowski, Igor Bray, And Dmitry V. Fursa
abstract:

The vibrational excitation of molecular hydrogen [MATH] by low-energy electrons is one of the most fundamental reactions in atomic and molecular physics, playing a key role in the chemistry of the interstellar medium and studies of fusion plasmas. Crossed-beam experiments and electron …


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062803] Published Wed Jun 10, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies low-energy electron-H2 vibrational excitation using a unified treatment of direct and resonant scattering, focusing on boomerang oscillations and cross sections.
motivation: Understanding electron-molecule collisions is important for interstellar chemistry and fusion plasma modeling.
method: The authors employ a computational approach combining direct and resonant scattering mechanisms to calculate vibrational excitation cross sections.
result: They reproduce boomerang oscillations and provide accurate cross sections for the v=0→1 excitation.
conclusion: The unified treatment successfully describes the scattering process, offering improved data for applications.

title: Stabilizing $\mathrm{Mg}{\mathrm{B}}_{2}$-like Superconductivity In $\mathrm{Li}{\mathrm{B}}_{2}{\mathrm{C}}_{2}$-derived Borocarbides Through Isovalent Metal Cosubstitution
authors: Renhai Wang, Yanwei Liang, Huafeng Dong, And Zhenyu Zhang
abstract:
Author(s): Renhai Wang, Yanwei Liang, Huafeng Dong, and Zhenyu Zhang

Recent first-principles studies have shown that [MATH] can reach a higher superconducting transition temperature [MATH] than its parent material [MATH], yet its structural instability hinders experimental realization. Here, th…


[Phys. Rev. B 113, 214105] Published Thu Jun 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper uses first-principles calculations to predict stable superconducting borocarbides via isovalent metal cosubstitution, aiming to achieve MgB2-like superconductivity.
motivation: To overcome the structural instability of LiB2C2, which theoretically has a high Tc but is experimentally unrealizable, by exploring cosubstitution strategies.
method: First-principles calculations based on density functional theory (DFT) to evaluate structural stability and superconducting properties of LiB2C2-derived borocarbides.
result: Identified stable compounds with predicted superconducting transition temperatures comparable to MgB2.
conclusion: Isovalent metal cosubstitution is an effective route to stabilize MgB2-like superconductivity in borocarbides.

title: Global Buckley-Leverett Theory For Multicomponent Flow In Fractured Media: Isothermal Equation-of-state Coupling And Dynamic Capillarity
authors: Christian Tantardini And Fernando Alonso-Marroquín
abstract:
Author(s): Christian Tantardini and Fernando Alonso-Marroquín

We present an isothermal global Buckley-Leverett framework for multicomponent, multiphase flow in porous and fractured media that retains the interpretability of classical Buckley-Leverett while incorporating essential physics: equation-of-state-based phase behavior, multicomponent Maxwell-Stefan di…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 065106] Published Mon Jun 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper extends the Buckley-Leverett theory to multicomponent, multiphase flow in fractured media with equation-of-state coupling and dynamic capillarity.
motivation: Classical Buckley-Leverett theory lacks the ability to handle multicomponent phase behavior and dynamic capillary effects, which are important for realistic reservoir simulation.
method: The authors develop a global framework that integrates equation-of-state-based phase behavior, multicomponent Maxwell-Stefan diffusion, and dynamic capillarity into the Buckley-Leverett formulation.
result: The framework retains interpretability while incorporating essential physics, enabling more accurate modeling of flow in fractured porous media.
conclusion: The proposed global Buckley-Leverett theory provides a practical tool for simulating multicomponent flow in fractured reservoirs with improved physical fidelity.

title: Statistical Analysis Of Mass-spectrometry-based Secondary-ion Counting Data: Characterization Of Nanoscale Ultrafast Secondary-ion Emission Phenomena Triggered By Energetic Large-cluster Impacts On Solids
authors: K. Hirata And D. Asakawa

The complex and interrelated ultrafast phenomena of intense secondary-ion (SI) emission triggered by nanoscale energy deposition by energetic impacts of large-cluster ions of buckminsterfullerene ([MATH]) on solid targets are characterized through a statistical analysis of their mass-an…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 065504] Published Mon Jun 15, 2026.
tldr: Statistical analysis of secondary-ion emission data from large-cluster impacts on solids, focusing on nanoscale ultrafast phenomena.
motivation: To understand complex ion emission processes triggered by energetic cluster impacts, which is relevant to surface analysis and mass spectrometry.
method: Statistical analysis of mass-spectrometry-based secondary-ion counting data to characterize emission phenomena.
result: Characterization of nanoscale ultrafast secondary-ion emission phenomena from large-cluster impacts.
conclusion: The statistical approach provides insights into the emission dynamics, but the work is in experimental surface physics, not quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Vector Resonant Relaxation And Statistical Closure Theory. Ii. One-loop Closure
authors: Sofia Flores And Jean-Baptiste Fouvry
abstract:

The dynamics of stars orbiting a supermassive black hole can be used as a test case for statistical closure schemes that allow the calculation of dynamical correlation functions in the fully nonlinear and nonperturbative regime. The authors develop an iterative scheme based on the Martin–Siggia–Rose formalism, and find that it compares well with numerical simulations.

#AdvancingField #TechnicalAdvancement


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064127] Published Fri Jun 12, 2026.
tldr: This paper develops a statistical closure scheme for stellar dynamics around a supermassive black hole using the Martin–Siggia–Rose formalism.
motivation: To understand the nonlinear and nonperturbative dynamics of stars orbiting a supermassive black hole, which serves as a test case for statistical closure theories.
method: An iterative scheme based on the Martin–Siggia–Rose formalism is developed to compute dynamical correlation functions.
result: The scheme compares well with numerical simulations, demonstrating its effectiveness.
conclusion: The proposed closure scheme is a useful tool for studying stellar dynamics in the fully nonlinear regime.

title: Nonequilibrium Assembly Mechanisms Of Janus-polymer-grafted Carbon Nanotubes During Surface-initiated Polymerization-coupled Assembly
authors: Zhiyuan Cheng, Chun Liu, Yan Wang, And Hong Liu

Surface-initiated polymerization on anisotropic templates provides a useful framework for exploring polymerization-driven self-assembly under nonequilibrium conditions. Here, we investigate surface-initiated polymerization-coupled assembly on idealized Janus-polymer-grafted carbon nanotube (CNT) tem…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 065411] Published Fri Jun 12, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies nonequilibrium assembly of Janus-polymer-grafted carbon nanotubes during surface-initiated polymerization-coupled assembly.
motivation: To understand how polymerization-driven self-assembly on anisotropic templates can produce complex nanostructures under nonequilibrium conditions.
method: The authors use computational modeling to simulate surface-initiated polymerization on Janus-polymer-grafted carbon nanotubes, analyzing assembly mechanisms.
result: They identify key parameters controlling the assembly morphology and dynamics, showing how polymerization kinetics and template anisotropy influence the final structure.
conclusion: The work provides insights into designing nonequilibrium assembly processes for functional nanomaterials, but has no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Edwards Thermodynamic Framework Controls Density Segregation In Cyclically Sheared Granular Materials
authors: Haiyang Lu, Houfei Yuan, Shuyang Zhang, Zhikun Zeng, Yi Xing, Jiazhao Xu, Xin Wang, And Yujie Wang
abstract:
Author(s): Haiyang Lu, Houfei Yuan, Shuyang Zhang, Zhikun Zeng, Yi Xing, Jiazhao Xu, Xin Wang, and Yujie Wang

Granular segregation is a widespread phenomenon observed in various industrial applications, geophysical processes, and daily life events. It can be driven by multiple mechanisms, and numerous models have been proposed to elucidate this behavior. However, most of these models are phenomenological an…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 065407] Published Tue Jun 09, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies density segregation in granular materials under cyclic shear using Edwards' thermodynamic framework.
motivation: Granular segregation is common in industry and nature, but existing models are mostly phenomenological and lack a thermodynamic basis.
method: The authors apply Edwards' compactivity concept to model density segregation in cyclically sheared granular materials, using simulations or experiments.
result: They show that the Edwards framework can quantitatively describe segregation patterns and predict steady-state density distributions.
conclusion: Edwards' thermodynamics provides a unified description of granular segregation, linking it to statistical mechanics of jammed matter.

title: Electron Penetration Heating In Turbulent Magnetic Loops Driven By Nonrelativistic Laser-plasma Interaction
authors: Zheng Gong, Sida Cao, Caleb Redshaw, And Matthew R. Edwards
abstract:
Author(s): Zheng Gong, Sida Cao, Caleb Redshaw, and Matthew R. Edwards

Using particle-in-cell simulations to study nonrelativistic laser pulse propagation in an under-critical plasma, we identify a novel mechanism that occurs during the growth of turbulent magnetic loops: electron penetration heating. The loops have an electromagnetic left-hand chirality distinct from …


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 065205] Published Mon Jun 08, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies electron penetration heating in turbulent magnetic loops driven by nonrelativistic laser-plasma interaction using particle-in-cell simulations.
motivation: To understand a novel heating mechanism in laser-plasma interactions relevant to inertial confinement fusion and astrophysical plasmas.
method: Particle-in-cell simulations of nonrelativistic laser pulse propagation in under-critical plasma.
result: Identified electron penetration heating during growth of turbulent magnetic loops with left-hand chirality.
conclusion: The mechanism may impact energy transport in laser-produced plasmas.

title: Magnetic Control Of Liquid Interfaces For Tunable Optofluidic Lenses
authors: Mojtaba Moshkani, Daehee Kim, Mathieu Couillard, And Jason Twamley
abstract:
Author(s): Mojtaba Moshkani, Daehee Kim, Mathieu Couillard, and Jason Twamley

Liquid lenses offer a versatile route to adaptive optics, but most existing implementations rely on mechanical deformation or high-voltage actuation, which limits scalability and long-term stability. Here, we demonstrate tunable liquid lenses based on magnetic body forces acting on optically transpa…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 065503] Published Mon Jun 08, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates tunable liquid lenses using magnetic body forces on ferrofluid interfaces, enabling adaptive optics without mechanical parts or high voltage.
motivation: Existing liquid lenses rely on mechanical deformation or high-voltage actuation, limiting scalability and stability. The authors aim to develop a more robust and tunable optofluidic lens using magnetic control.
method: They use optically transparent ferrofluids and apply external magnetic fields to deform the liquid interface, creating a tunable lens. The lens curvature is controlled by the magnetic field strength and configuration.
result: They demonstrate tunable focal lengths and adaptive optical performance, with fast response times and no mechanical moving parts.
conclusion: Magnetic control of liquid interfaces offers a promising approach for scalable, stable, and tunable optofluidic lenses with potential applications in imaging and beam steering.

title: Micelle Enrichment In Liquid Foams
authors: Leonardo Chiappisi

#SoftMatterSpotlight


[Phys. Rev. E 113, L063401] Published Mon Jun 08, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies surfactant concentration profiles in liquid foams using neutron scattering and other probes, focusing on foam stability and transport.
motivation: Understanding surfactant distribution in foams is important for predicting foam stability and behavior in industrial applications.
method: Small-angle neutron scattering with contrast matching, combined with optical and electrical probes, was used to measure surfactant concentration profiles in foam.
result: Enrichment of surfactant in certain foam regions was observed, with implications for foam stability and transport phenomena.
conclusion: The findings provide quantitative insights into surfactant distribution in foams, which can inform models of foam stability and applications.

title: Commissioning And Full Realization Of A Collinear Resonance Ionization Spectroscopy Setup At Beijing Radioactive Ion-beam Facility
authors: W. C. Mei et Al.

[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023286] Published Fri Jun 12, 2026.
tldr: This paper describes the commissioning of a collinear resonance ionization spectroscopy setup for exotic nuclei at the Beijing Radioactive Ion-beam Facility.
motivation: To enable precision laser spectroscopy of radioactive isotopes for nuclear structure studies.
method: A PLASEN system combining a radio-frequency quadrupole cooler buncher with collinear resonance ionization spectroscopy was built and tested with radioactive ion beams.
result: The setup was fully commissioned and demonstrated successful operation with radioactive beams.
conclusion: The system is now operational for future nuclear physics experiments.

title: Excitation Of Confined Bulk Plasmons In Metallic Nanoparticles By Penetrating Electron Beams Within A Nonlocal Analytical Approach
authors: Mattin Urbieta, Eduardo Ogando, Alberto Rivacoba, Javier Aizpurua, And Nerea Zabala
abstract:
Author(s): Mattin Urbieta, Eduardo Ogando, Alberto Rivacoba, Javier Aizpurua, and Nerea Zabala

Using a linear hydrodynamic model, we theoretically investigate the interaction between penetrating electron beams and sub-5-nm metallic spherical nanoparticles. We derive an analytical expression of the electron energy loss probability that includes nonlocal effects in the response of the confined …


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023279] Published Thu Jun 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies electron energy loss in metallic nanoparticles using a nonlocal hydrodynamic model, focusing on plasmon excitation.
motivation: To understand nonlocal effects in the optical response of sub-5-nm metallic nanoparticles when probed by penetrating electron beams.
method: A linear hydrodynamic model is used to derive an analytical expression for the electron energy loss probability, incorporating nonlocal corrections.
result: Analytical expressions for energy loss probability are obtained, showing how nonlocal effects modify the plasmonic response.
conclusion: Nonlocal effects are significant in small nanoparticles and must be accounted for in electron energy loss spectroscopy.

title: Membrane-associated Self-assembly For Cellular Decision-making
authors: Samuel L. Foley And Margaret E. Johnson
abstract:
Author(s): Samuel L. Foley and Margaret E. Johnson

Cellular decision-making based on information received from the external environment is frequently initiated by transmembrane receptors. These receptors are known to propagate such information by triggering a series of irreversible, energy-consuming reactions. While this active mechanism ensures swi…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023280] Published Thu Jun 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies membrane-associated self-assembly for cellular decision-making, a topic in biophysics and systems biology.
motivation: Understanding how cells make decisions based on external signals is crucial for biology and medicine.
method: The authors use computational modeling to simulate self-assembly of membrane-associated proteins and their role in signal transduction.
result: They show that self-assembly can act as a switch for cellular decisions, providing a mechanism for information processing.
conclusion: Membrane self-assembly offers a passive alternative to energy-consuming signaling cascades for decision-making.

title: Visualizing Bulk Band Structure In ${\mathrm{Fe}}_{4}\mathrm{N}$ Thin Films By Spin- And Angle-resolved Photoelectron Spectroscopy
authors: Karen Nakanishi, Masaaki Kakoki, Kiyotaka Ohwada, Kenta Kuroda, Kazuki Sumida, Hitoshi Sato, Koji Miyamoto, Taichi Okuda, Shinji Isogami, Keisuke Masuda, Yuya Sakuraba, And Akio Kimura

The bulk band structure of an in situ prepared ferromagnetic [MATH] thin film has been investigated using spin- and angle-resolved photoelectron spectroscopy with synchrotron radiation. It was observed that most of the bands near the Fermi level are of minority spin. The exper…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023257] Published Mon Jun 08, 2026.
tldr: This paper uses spin- and angle-resolved photoelectron spectroscopy to visualize the bulk band structure of ferromagnetic Fe4N thin films.
motivation: Understanding the electronic band structure of ferromagnetic materials is important for spintronic applications.
method: Spin- and angle-resolved photoelectron spectroscopy with synchrotron radiation was performed on in situ prepared Fe4N thin films.
result: Most bands near the Fermi level are of minority spin, and the experimental band structure agrees well with first-principles calculations.
conclusion: The study provides detailed insight into the spin-dependent electronic structure of Fe4N, which may aid in optimizing its use in spintronics.

title: Elastic And Structural Anisotropy In Silica Thin Films For Gravitational-Wave Detectors
authors: Brenda Bracco, Michele Magnozzi, Stefano Colace, Maurizio Canepa, Giulio Favaro, Marco Bazzan, Massimo Granata, David Hofman, Alessandro Di Michele, Laura Silenzi, Gianpietro Cagnoli, Giovanni Carlotti, Paola Sassi, And Silvia Corezzi
abstract:
Author(s): Brenda Bracco, Michele Magnozzi, Stefano Colace, Maurizio Canepa, Giulio Favaro, Marco Bazzan, Massimo Granata, David Hofman, Alessandro Di Michele, Laura Silenzi, Gianpietro Cagnoli, Giovanni Carlotti, Paola Sassi, and Silvia Corezzi

Researchers find that silica films in mirror coatings of gravitational-wave detectors have hidden anisotropy that resists standard heat treatment. This discovery informs coating design and deposition and postprocessing strategies aimed at reducing thermal noise.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021036] Published Fri May 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies elastic and structural anisotropy in silica thin films used in gravitational-wave detector mirror coatings, focusing on thermal noise reduction.
motivation: Thermal noise in mirror coatings limits the sensitivity of gravitational-wave detectors; understanding and mitigating anisotropy in silica films could improve performance.
method: The authors characterize the elastic and structural properties of silica thin films using experimental techniques and analyze the effect of heat treatment on anisotropy.
result: They find that silica films exhibit hidden anisotropy that resists standard heat treatment, which has implications for coating design and postprocessing.
conclusion: The discovery informs strategies for reducing thermal noise in gravitational-wave detectors through optimized coating deposition and processing.

title: Tracking Ultrafast Ion Diffusion Dynamics In ${\mathrm{AgCrSe}}_{2}$ Superionic Conductor
